I would also like to make the assumption that, in speaking on behalf of the Government on third reading of this Bill, the Deputy Prime Minister will be the only speaker for the Government today. On that assumption I can assure him that I will be the only speaker for Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition on this Bill today. I would expect the same arrangement would prevail with the New Democratic Party.

June 28, 1984
International Peace and Security
I too want to compliment the members of the Standing Committee, particularly the Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens), who worked so assiduously to achieve the amendments of which the Deputy Prime Minister spoke and which have vastly improved the Bill.
Immediately prior to the Bill's receiving second reading in the House last May 11, I put before Members what I believed was the agreement between the Government and my Party with respect to Bill C-32, an Act to establish the Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security. As Members know, and as spokesmen for our Party have made clear in debate and before committee, we welcome the establishment of this Institute. Indeed, our Leader indicated to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) last April 9, after receiving the draft Bill from the Prime Minister, that the requirement in Canada for institutional restructuring and innovation in this field is beyond question. However, as was made clear to the Government both before and after Bill C-32 was introduced into the House, we viewed the Bill as proposed to be fatally flawed in respect of the lack of independence of the centre, its lack of accountability to Parliament, and the politically negative effect that private funding of the centre might have on existing indigenous centres of research.
I need not refer today to the lengthy and very productive exchanges between the Prime Minister and my Leader which led the Government to support substantial amendments to this Bill prior to its receiving second reading support last May 11. These amendments would strengthen the independence and integrity of the Institute and provide for an appointment process which would leave no room for doubt that the board of directors would be non-partisan and would enjoy the confidence and support of all Parties. At that time I was able to report to the House, as reported at page 3656 of Hansard, the three main points of agreement between the Government and Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition. Hansard reads:
First, the Government has accepted the suggestion of the Leader of the Opposition that consultations on the composition of the board of directors start immediately, especially with respect to the appointment of the chairman and the executive director, as they will be key appointments for establishing the tone and quality of the institute. Second, the Government has agreed to immediate consultation with national organizations and interested Canadians with respect to receiving nominations for the board of directors. It is our expectation, as I know it to be the Prime Minister's, that there will be full agreement on the composition of the board of directors prior to the end of committee consideration of the Bill. Third, concurrent with this consultation, the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence will be examining the Bill and recommending a formal list of national organizations which, once the Bill is passed, will become the pool from which nominees for the board of directors will be selected.
I believe this process has been respected and that consultations have been meaningful, that Canadians have participated fully in the selection of candidates for the board of directors and that the process itself has underscored the independence and integrity of the Institute.
In committee the Government presented the full and detailed amendments to which I reported agreement last May 11 and which we now have before us today.
With respect to the selection of the board of directors, the Deputy Prime Minister and I began consultations on May 25 with a view to reaching agreement on the board of directors prior to the end of committee consideration of the Bill. At that time, on behalf of my Leader, I recommended to the Deputy Prime Minister the following criteria in considering candidates for the chairmanship and executive directorship of the Institute, criteria which would enhance, I believe, the integrity and independence of the board: first, it is imperative that we consider the chairmanship and executive directorship together as a team; second, we would recommend that no present bureaucrats be considered for either position; third, it is important that the executive director in particular have academic credibility; four, these appointments should reflect concern for and competence in both disarmament and security matters; five, we would like to consider a woman for at least one of these positions.
I was most pleased when the Deputy Prime Minister put into play candidates who clearly met these criteria, and on behalf of my Leader I indicated that our Party would have no objection to these nominees.
With respect to the board of directors, at a meeting with the Deputy Prime Minister on June 1, I suggested the following criteria for selection of candidates, again with a view to enhancing the independence and integrity of the Institute: first, they should be broadly representative of the existing indigenous research community. Second, they should be nominated from the pool of recommendations the committee is receiving. Third, as the Minister for External Relations (Mr. Pepin) stated in the House, the board should not include any serving bureaucrats. Fourth, the board should include at least five women. Fifth, while the Act provides for up to seven foreign directors, we would recommend that initially there be no more than three. Six, that there be a geographical and language balance.
Current with our discussions, the Standing Committee and the Secretary of State for External Affairs initiated a detailed consultative process with national organizations and interest groups to elicit their nomination for the Board. Out of this list, and respecting the criteria outlined above, the Deputy Prime Minister wrote to me on June 12 and proposed the list which he has presented to the House today. It will not be necessary for me to go over that list in my remarks.
After reviewing this list with my Leader, I reported to the Deputy Prime Minister that my Party had no objection to the nominees as put forward by the Government. It is our expectation that the Government will continue to act in good faith and adhere to these nominees. Should any nominee withdraw his or her nomination, we would expect the Government to re-establish the consultation process with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) until such time as the first board of directors is in place. And it is on this basis that my Party gives its approval to this Bill.
I next received a call from the Deputy Prime Minister on June 21 indicating that consensus could not be reached at this time respecting the Government's nominee for executive direc-
June 28, 1984

tor, and the Deputy Prime Minister suggested an alternate course which, if acceptable, would preserve the integrity of the board without putting into jeopardy the substantial agreement between the Government and Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition. Specifically, he suggested that the Government nominate the board of directors as I have outlined and leave to the board itself the election of a chairman and executive director out of the existing membership. To ensure that such voting was done only by the Canadian-based nominees, any foreign-based nominations would not be made until after the selection of the chairman and executive director had been completed.
I am grateful to the Deputy Prime Minister today for his putting on the record the commitment of the future Prime Minister to honour the undertakings as presented to the House today. While this was a change from our earlier understanding, I indicated to the Deputy Prime Minister that we would have no objection to this procedure.
The committee has now reported on the Bill and the amendments reflect the points of agreement I have described to the House.
The establishment of a Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security is a substantial achievement. It is fitting that it should have been the subject of the Deputy Prime Minister's speech today, it being in all likelihood the last one he will be making to the House.
I am happy to acknowledge that the Bill before us today represents a substantial improvement to the original draft Bill. This is a tribute to the Government and to the Leader of the Opposition. I commend them for their genuine contribution to achieving a process which has enhanced the integrity and independence of the Institute.
Now, as the Institute is formed and in its early days, we must all continue to be vigilant so that the gains which have been made over the past number of months might continue to characterize the Institute. We have the genesis of a world-class Institute with integrity and with public support.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I almost had a catch in my throat when the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), in his speech today, said that it would probably be his last speech since he will not be running again for a seat in the House of Commons. We may see him at the U.N. or perhaps in the Senate, but we are bound to see him again. Many of us are sorry that we will not see him here.
I am pleased that in what is probably his last speech he was able to speak on this extremely important Bill to create a Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security.
I would also like to say that we in this Party have been very appreciative of the efforts made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) as well as the Secretary of State for External Affairs to create this Institute. I think it is largely owing to the zeal of the Prime Minister that such an Institute should be created that we now have the Bill before us. I suggest that the award
International Peace and Security of the Albert Einstein peace prize to the Prime Minister the other day is a tribute to the efforts he has made in his pilgrimage of peace. More importantly, I feel that he is leaving a lasting contribution as a result of the Bill we are discussing today.
The Minister has had to do much of the work in consultations with the House Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party, with my Leader and myself to bring the Bill to its present excellent form. May I say, Mr. Speaker, he has also been assisted enormously by the Chairman of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence. That Hon. Member showed great patience and understanding throughout the very long and somewhat strained deliberations in committee. The fact that the Bill should now be in the House for third reading is due in no small measure to the excellent conduct of the committee by its Chairman. I know he is not leaving politics, but if he were this too would be a very fitting tribute to him to have accomplished so much.
I think we should once again recall the title of the Bill and the name of the new Institute, the Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security. Some of us in this Party would have liked to put in the word "research" and called it the Canadian Research Institute for International Peace and Security, but that was not approved by a majority in the committee. As one reads the purpose of the Bill as newly defined, one sees that a good deal of its purpose will embody the fostering of research.
It is the other part of the title of the Institute that I want to say a word or two about. It is an Institute for International Peace and Security. The word "international" prefaces both peace and security. We are talking about international peace and international security. It brings to mind the efforts that were made by people like Olof Palme and the members of the Palme Commission a few years ago when they were studying disarmament issues and who coined the phrase "a common security". When they talk about security, they are not talking about it in terms of each nation building up its defences, each nation vying with others to be as militarily strong or, if possible, superior to others. Not at all. They are talking about, and I think it is implicit in the new Canadian Institute title, a common security, the wish of all of us to reach a position where there is international security which is a common security. It is therefore extremely important for me, at any rate, and for members of this Party that the Institute should be dedicated both to international peace and international security.
We feel that the purpose clause as studied and drafted and redrafted has come through very strongly indeed, taking many of the ideas brought to us by witnesses before the committee and from many of the submissions made to the committee. Perhaps since other speakers have not mentioned it, let me put on the record the purpose clause, which is Clause 4 of the Bill. It reads:

June 28, 1984
International Peace and Security
4. The purpose of the Institute is to increase knowledge and understanding of the issues relating to international peace and security from a Canadian perspective, with particular emphasis on arms control, disarmament, defence and conflict resolution, and to
(a)	foster, fund and conduct research on matters relating to international peace and security;
(b)	promote scholarship in matters relating to international peace and security;
(c)	study and propose ideas and policies for the enhancement of international peace and security;
(d)	collect and disseminate information on, and encourage public discussion of, issues of international peace and security.
Other important amendments were made to the Bill, some proposed by the Government and some proposed by the Opposition Parties. I would mention particularly the enhancement of the role of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence and the strengthening of broad and general parliamentary oversight. Some amendments we would have liked to see did not get through. We would have liked at least half of the board of directors to be women and we are sorry that in this first list only four are women. The reason I mention that particularly, Mr. Speaker, is that from the Voice of Women onwards Canadian women have played such an incredibly important and strong role in the peace and disarmament movement in this country. I would only hope subsequent appointments will show a greater recognition of their enormous efforts of these many decades.
One puzzle that remains, and the Minister in reply to my question did not entirely resolve it, is if the board of directors, after it chooses its chairman from among its number-and it seems quite appropriate that it choose its chairman from among its number-should decide that it would like to look outside its membership for an executive director, it is not entirely clear yet to me that it can do so. At the meeting of the standing committee, the Minister implied that it could do so, and in answer to my question today he still left the door slightly ajar for that to be possible. But I would have liked that point to have been made more explicit.
It seems to me the position of executive director is absolutely crucial to the success of the Institute. A search should be made to ensure that the very strongest and best Canadian be chosen for this position. The best way would be for the 14 Canadian members of the board to establish a search committee, a very common practice in the academic world, to receive and accept applications for executive director. Then this committee would conduct a series of hearings with such nominees in order to ensure that the very best executive director is chosen. If a person outside the board were so chosen, then by the Governor in Council that person would be made a member of the board. This would then raise the board membership to 15, leaving two spaces for non-Canadians. When the Minister is talking with members of the board, the first 14, I hope he will make it clear that that oportunity is open to them. We have had many discussions, the Minister and I, about the very important role of the executive director and about the kind of person who might well be chosen for that position. I know that many members of the disarmament community have also given this matter a great deal of thought and have provided a great
deal of input as to the kind of executive director they think would be best for a Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security.
I hope it is clearly understood that the 14 Canadian directors could indeed establish such a search committee, go outside their number, find a person they consider best for the position of executive director, and have that executive director then made a member of the board.
I am worried that the amended Clause 7 does not provide for this. It indicates that the first executive director shall be elected by the board from among its members, yet the Minister indicated in committee that the first executive director could be chosen in the way which I have just outlined and then be made a member of the board. I am assuming that this is possible.
We in this Party are very glad that the Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security is to become a reality before the end of this session of Parliament. We have been glad to assist in a variety of ways, which I hope have been helpful to the Minister and to the chairman of the committee, to ensure that the Institute would be a world-class Institute and that it would at least have sufficient funds to get started. We are very supportive of all the efforts which I know the board will make to ensure that the Institute is the world-class Institute we all want it to be.

Mr. Speaker, I thank you for giving me the opportunity to say a few words on this most important Bill. When I spoke to it on April 18 at second reading, I said the following:
Mr. Speaker, as the culmination of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) peace initiative we have before us Bill C-32, an Act to establish the Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security. The principles involved in this legislation are sound. Let us cease this ongoing nitpicking and send this legislation to committee where we can adjust the language and change "shalls" to "mays" if advisable. Let us get on with this legislation. With regard to the principles behind this legislation, we need only ask whether it is needed, what its dimensions are to be, and where the institute shall be located.
The Bill has been considered extensively in committee. Many people appeared before the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence to express their views. Some amendments to the Bill have been made. I am pleased that the Bill will be passed before we adjourn tomorrow.
I want to say again that I support the Bill, but let no one think that the proposed Institute will solve the conflicts of the world or, for that matter, reduce in the short term present tensions between the two superpowers of the world. However, it is a breath of fresh air in the world process of dialogue and study toward world peace. In particular, it may be some help in building the bridge of reason, discussion and accord between our two mighty neighbours to the south and to the north of us. Again I say let us locate this Institute in western Canada as a beginning of that bridge between our two neighbours.
International Peace and Security
In closing, I wish the retiring Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) well in his future endeavours. I suggest to him that he should wear his kilt more often; it is becoming.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to introduce second reading of Bill C-43, a Bill to establish in law the Canada-Nova Scotia Offshore Oil and Gas Agreement. As Members will recall, the Canada-Nova Scotia Offshore Oil Agreement was signed on March 2, 1982. Legislation to ensure the full implementation of the agreement was introduced in this House and in the Nova Scotia Legislature on May 31, 1984.
Bill C-43 establishes in law the major elements of the agreement, a co-operative regime to manage offshore petroleum activity and a revenue-sharing regime that ensures the province reaps the lion's share of benefits in this activity.
This legislation, and the Canada-Nova Scotia Agreement which led to it, are excellent examples of federal-provincial co-operation. Both were achieved in a climate of close and positive negotiation. Major benefits have already accrued to the province. Since March, 1982 33 exploration agreements worth more than $2.4 billion have been negotiated. In 1983 approximately $150 million was directly invested in Nova Scotia by the offshore petroleum industry. About 2,000 jobs have been created in Nova Scotia by offshore petroleum activity, and another several hundred resulting from the multiplier effect such job creation produces.
Two hundred companies in Nova Scotia are now involved in the offshore effort. Many of these are local firms that specialize in marine and logistical services as well as fabrication. Others have moved to Nova Scotia to establish businesses and
employ Nova Scotians. These are real achievements made in just two years. The legislation before us will implement the Agreement that contributed to them and ensure that these benefits continue to accrue to Nova Scotia for many years to come.
The concept underlying the implementation of the Canada-Nova Scotia Agreement is unique in the history of federal-provincial relations. Both governments have agreed to put aside their respective claims to jurisdiction over the offshore and to introduce complementary legislation to implement a common, unified system for revenues and the joint management of petroleum activity.

subtopic: CANADA-NOVA SCOTIA OIL AND GAS AGREEMENT ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the legislation before us today, Bill C-43, will make the interim Canada-Nova Scotia Offshore Oil and Gas Board a permanent institution with legal authority to manage petroleum activity in the offshore Nova Scotia area. Both Ministers will delegate substantial authority to the Board. Where authority is retained at the ministerial level, complementary delegation by the two federal and provincial Ministers to one another as appropriate will ensure a unified regime.
The operation of the interim Board over the past two years has been completely satisfactory to both Canada and Nova Scotia. Not once in those two years has there been a need to use the mechanisms dealing with conflict resolution. Agreement has always been achieved through positive discussion. The makeup of the interim Board will remain unchanged as it gains the status of a permanent body. The reason for this is quite simple. Why change a good thing when it is working? The Administrator of the Canada Oil and Gas Lands Administration will continue to be the Board's chairperson and the federal Government will continue to have two additional representatives on the Board, as will the provincial Government.
Under the authority set by this Bill, the Board will be responsible for managing oil and gas activity everywhere off the coast of Nova Scotia. However, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources will be empowered to accept or modify a decision of the Board. The Minister will also be able to make a decision in the absence of one made by the Board providing he or she has asked for one from the Board. The federal Minister will delegate to the Nova Scotia Minister of Mines and Energy ultimate authority for management of the Bay of Fundy, Sable Island and its "footprint", the shallow area around the island. The federal Minister will retain ultimate authority in all other offshore areas where significant or commercial discoveries or projects overlap the Sable Island "footprint" and the rest of the offshore. Both Ministers will have the authority to execute
Canada-Nova Scotia Oil Agreement decisions. The delegation will also provide that each Minister will be able to delay decisions relating to the other's areas of ultimate authority.
These management provisions are important for two reasons. First, they ensure that both federal and provincial interests are protected. Second, they provide the petroleum industry with the certainty it needs to proceed with development. We fully expect that the Board will continue to make decisions on the basis of a consensus, as it has done without exception, for more than two years.
One aspect of Bill C-43 that is particularly important is the formula to share revenues from the offshore. The legislation ensures that Nova Scotia will receive the lion's share of offshore petroleum revenues. In fact, in the early years of the agreement, the province will receive substantially more revenues than if it owned the resource on land. There will be wider sharing of revenues only if the province's relative fiscal capacity-that is, its capacity to raise revenues from taxation and from revenue-sharing agreements with the federal Government-exceeds that of almost all other provinces.
Until Nova Scotia's per capita fiscal capacity reaches 110 per cent of the national average-adjusted upward by two percentage points for every one percentage point that the province's unemployment rate exceeds the national average- the province will receive all offshore revenue, including a major federal tax, the petroleum and gas revenue tax, but excluding the federal share of the corporate income tax.
These revenues are substantial. They include the basic royalty; the progressive incremental royalty; bonus payments and licence fees; revenues that are equivalent to a provincial-type corporate tax and retail sales tax in the offshore region; and, the federal petroleum and gas revenue tax. All of these revenues collected from the Bay of Fundy and from Sable Island and its "footprint" will go to the provincial government, no matter how high its fiscal capacity.
The federal Government will begin to share in revenues from other areas of the offshore only when the province's per capita fiscal capacity exceeds the 110 per cent level, adjusted by the unemployment factor. In the meantime, a Nova Scotia Offshore Oil and Gas Revenue Fund will be established by the federal Government to collect the province's share of the revenues.
Some concern has been expressed about the impact this agreement will have on equalization payments to Nova Scotia. I want to assure Hon. Members that Bill C-43 contains special measures to ensure that Nova Scotia experiences real net increases in its revenues. In accordance with the principle upon which the equalization scheme is based, equalization payments to Nova Scotia will be reduced as the province's fiscal capacity increases because of offshore petroleum revenue. However, Bill C-43 contains a special provision to protect the provincial government from a situation in which it loses a dollar of equalization for every dollar of offshore petroleum revenue. Under Bill C-43, Nova Scotia will be reimbursed for much of
80152 44

June 28, 1984
Canada-Nova Scotia Oil Agreement the reduction in equalization payments. In fact, the province will be protected for up to ten years from the full effects of reductions as it gains offshore revenues.
A third aspect of this legislation which I would like to address is the provision to allow the Government of Nova Scotia to purchase up to 50 per cent of any Crown share in a natural gas field, and 25 per cent in an oil field. It is important to note that this special clause in no way changes the Crown share provisions of the Canada Oil and Gas Act. Rather, it deals with how the Crown share is divided between the federal and provincial governments.
Bill C-43 also provides for the establishment of a $200 million development fund to help Nova Scotia defray some of the costs of providing an infrastructure for offshore petroleum activity. Basically, this fund will assist Nova Scotia in putting in place the kinds of facilities and services necessary for the province to take maximum advantage of offshore petroleum opportunities. The fund will be made available in four annual instalments of $50 million. Nova Scotia will start to repay the $200 million only in the third year after substantial natural gas or oil production begins in the offshore.
I would like to take a few brief minutes to address some of the other special provisions which are contained in the legislation. For example, the Bill will require petroleum companies negotiating exploration agreements for offshore Nova Scotia to submit a plan which shows, to the satisfaction of the Canada-Nova Scotia Board, how the province's residents will benefit from the activity. Companies involved in exploration projects will be required to show how they propose to employ Nova Scotians in all aspects of their work. They will also be required to provide manufacturers, consultants, contractors and service companies based in Nova Scotia with a full and fair opportunity to compete in the supply of goods and services to an exploration program. Further, companies will be required to submit programs satisfactory to both governments for training, education and research, and technology.
Finally, before being sold elsewhere, oil and gas produced in offshore Nova Scotia will be made available in the province to satisfy consumer needs and to serve as a feedstock for existing industries. New industrial facilities will also be ensured of the availability of those feedstocks in excess of that needed to meet the demand of the existing industrial capacity in eastern Canada.
I am confident that the Members of this House will support this new legislation because it provides a co-operative and workable way of managing the offshore and a generous revenue-sharing system that ensures major, long-term benefits to the Province of Nova Scotia.

You are quite correct, Mr. Speaker.
Premier Buchanan in his communication said, and I quote:
The Government of Nova Scotia, while not having sufficient time to totally assess the proposal, has read it with great interest and is most impressed with your attitude. The idea of an Atlantic Canada oil and gas policy is one which we would be interested in discussing in more detail.
In our discussions, Premier Buchanan has acknowledged the Atlantic offshore accord to be both unique and, in his words, equitable in its approach to both revenue sharing and to the administration and management of the resource. The Government of Nova Scotia has, of course, already passed its mirror legislation regarding this Bill before the House today, but under the terms of that Act the Government of Nova Scotia could exercise its right to accept any elements of a further agreement negotiated with the Government of Newfoundland or, presumably, any other offshore province.
For the record, let us establish the 15 points of the Atlantic offshore accord as it would apply to Nova Scotia. The first heading is "Management". Point one: we recognize the legitimate desire of Nova Scotia to ensure that the pace and manner of development maximizes the social and economic benefits to the province. We will be prepared to establish a system of management which recognizes Nova Scotia's right to share in the control of all aspects of resource development.
Point two: the principle of joint management will be achieved by the establishment of a joint agency consisting of three representatives of the federal Government, three representatives of the provincial Government, and a mutually acceptable independent chairman.
Point three: our agreement will give this agency clear and precise management criteria which will govern the exercise of each Government's authority in areas specified in the legislation.
Point four: federal jurisdiction with regard to environmental protection under the Fisheries Act, the Canada Shipping Act, and other areas of federal jurisdiction, would not be affected.
Point five: a further principle concerns the protection of Nova Scotia workers and, especially, Nova Scotia's traditional industry, the fishery. Such protection will be ensured by the application of the province's social legislation to the offshore.
Point six: if either the agency or Ministers fail to reach agreement, a suspensive veto provision will apply. In the national interest, the federal Government will have the ultimate decision in matters affecting the pace and mode of exploration and the pace of production until national self-sufficiency is reached or if self-sufficiency and security of supply has been lost. There will be an independent, objective determi-

June 28, 1984
Canada-Nova Scotia Oil Agreement nation of what constitutes self-sufficiency and security of supply. The province would have the ultimate decision in matters affecting the mode of development or the actual development plan, subject to a federal override which would only apply if the province's choice, as determined by an independent objective process, delayed unreasonably the attainment of self-sufficiency and security of supply.
The second heading of the Atlantic accord is entitled "Revenue Sharing". Point seven: we believe that the principle of revenue sharing between the federal and provincial levels should be the same for all oil and gas producing regions, without discrimination. Therefore, Nova Scotia will be entitled to establish and collect resource revenues as if these resources were on land. The federal Government will maintain the right to establish and collect federal taxes, where appropriate. Federal and provincial taxes of general application, such as the corporate income taxes and sales taxes, will apply.
Point eight: offshore oil will be included in the category of hydrocarbon resources which attract market-sensitive prices.
Point nine: a Progressive Conservative administration would agree to establish a joint offshore development fund in order to provide an accelerated revenue flow to help finance infrastructure required to bring the resource onstream.
Point ten: if, on assuming office, the new Government decides to vest in itself the Crown-carried shares of offshore Nova Scotia, then these rights and shares will be shared equitably by both Governments.
Point 11: local job creation and labour development would be of paramount concern. Oil-related infrastructure could be expanded and the offices of oil companies, including, where possible, Petro-Canada and federal departments, dealing with Nova Scotia offshore and the staff of the joint agency, would be located in the province.
Point 12: upgrading of infrastructure facilities in relation to the offshore would begin as soon as possible, following the signing of an agreement.
Point 13: it is important that there should be no dollar for dollar loss of equalization payments as a result of offshore revenues flowing to the province. The current equalization provisions will apply. Nova Scotia would receive offset payments from the federal Government equal to 90 per cent of a year's reduction in equalization payments. Beginning in the fifth year of production, this offset rate would be reduced by 10 per cent for each subsequent year.
Point 14: we believe that the question concerning ownership is secondary to control of the resources and the wealth they will produce. Should the Province of Nova Scotia or any other province wish to propose a constitutional amendment concerning an entrenchment of the offshore agreement, and if the necessary number of other provinces agree, as is provided for in the Canada Act, a Progressive Conservative Government will propose to Parliament the appropriate amendment.
Point 15: it is proposed that an agreement would be concluded immediately following the formation of a Progressive Conservative Government, with legislation being introduced within a reasonable period thereafter and, in any case, not more than one year. In announcing the agreement in principle in St. John's, the Conservative Leader said:
We want the energy policy to be a unifying force in Canada-not an instrument of division so favoured by the Liberals.
He told his audience:
This commitment today is an indication that new attitudes and new approaches to common problems can transform them swiftly into splendid opportunities for economic growth and prosperity.
In comparison, the legislation before the House today can be categorized as rigid, centralized and discriminatory. Rigid, because of the various formulas used for revenue sharing. Centralized, because management rests with the federal Government. Discriminatory, because the Atlantic Provinces are treated differently from the western oil and gas producing provinces. That is why we say our proposal is a better deal and that is why we will be introducing it before this House when we are in government. That is why Premier Brian Peckford, in accepting the agreement in principle for Newfoundland, said:
Both sides approached the issue in good faith with a genuine desire to reach a mutually satisfactory agreement and the process was successful.
That is why Newfoundlanders gave the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) 14 standing ovations and why they cheered him from the balconies of the House of Assembly.
The accord we have reached, which has been offered to the other provinces, is respectful of Canadian constitutional law, protective of national energy priorities, and sensitive to the social and economic needs of the people of Atlantic Canada. As I said, it was conducted in full consultation with the Premiers and energy ministers of the other provinces. It provides for a fair share of offshore revenues and for a real and positive role by both governments in the management of the development of the offshore resource. We firmly believe that the offshore will be an important building block for Canada in the years ahead, particularly Atlantic Canada. In coming to this agreement we are showing that Canadians are willing and able to listen to each other, to identify concerns and act together in a common cause.
Although we support Nova Scotia's effort in winning any concessions over the offshore in these dying days of a dying Liberal Government, there is one feature of this Bill which is repugnant to our Party and which should be repugnant to all Canadians. That, of course, is the retroactive back-in, which effectively appropriates without compensation exploration and production rights previously issued. This retroactive back-in was introduced in the Liberal Government's national energy policy.
It is repugnant because it is the action of a country which cannot or will not keep its commitments. Investors around the world lost confidence in Canada because the rules of the game were changed after the investment was made and the property right acquired. Our Party is firmly on record in its opposition to the retroactive back-in component of the Crown share. The
June 28, 1984

Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson), the Hon. Member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) and the Hon. Member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) and other members of our caucus have been adamant in voicing our opposition to what amounts to straight theft. The Leader of the Opposition, in one of his first statements on energy policy, said:
The federal action resembled nothing more than a hold up at a corner gas station at 3 a.m.
There is so much obvious retroactivity and confiscation in the NEP that investors lost whatever trust and confidence they had in the federal government. Simply put, they would no longer make long-term commitments because they had no longer believed that the Government would honour its own undertakings.
Opponents of the retroactive back-in claim that expropriation without compensation violates Canada's obligations under international law. The concept that Canadians would welch on their word and tear up old agreements led to an unprecedented outflow of capital from Canada following the introduction of the NEP. Billions of dollars held by both residents and nonresidents fled the country seeking more secure and stable investment climates. The damage caused by the retroactive feature of the back-in may never be fully measured in terms of the lost opportunities this punitive measure denied.
In discussing the retroactive back-in it is important to note the difference between providing for Canadian participation and retroactively expropriating property without compensation. The Conservative Party fully supports the concept that Canadians should participate in the wealth of oil and gas resources. Other countries such as Norway and Britain have reserved for their own right a share of the production of the oil and gas wealth. But it is critical that such intentions be announced at the time the exploration and drilling rights are being acquired, and therefore known in advance to all parties concerned. When the oil and gas industry is investing billions of dollars, much of it raised from Canadian investors, the industry simply wants to know the rules of the game and they wish some assurance that the rules will not be changed retroactively. That is the effect of the retroactive back-in.
The second point deals with the back-in provisions in the legislation now before the House. There is some confusion in the oil industry with regard to the reference to the back-in in the Act, and I gather some confusion on the part of the Government which wishes to propose an amendment to this point. The retroactive back-in is not necessarily enshrined in the legislation before us. It was introduced in Bill C-48, the Canada Oil and Gas Act. As Premier John Buchanan points out, the Bill before us simply provides for Nova Scotia's participation in the event that the back-in clause is ever activated. It is important to note that it has never been exercised because it applies to the acquisition of production rights, and the oil and gas discoveries affected by the back-in are still a long way from production.
This Act s'imply states that, prior to transferring or disposing of any Crown share in the offshore region, the Nova Scotia Government shall have the right to acquire a 50 per cent portion of the Crown share in respect of the natural gas field, and a 25 per cent portion of the Crown share in respect of an
Canada-Nova Scotia Oil Agreement
oil field. In other words, Nova Scotia is saying that if the federal Government picks up a share of the action in the offshore production game, it wants a piece of the action.
In contrast, under the terms of the Atlantic offshore accord, there would be no need for a retroactive back-in because the accord permits any province to impose any revenue regime it desires on the offshore resource. If the revenue regime is uneconomic, the oil and gas development will not proceed. The onus is on the province as well as the federal Government to ensure that the fiscal terms make that development viable.
Some Liberal opponents in the Atlantic region say that the Conservatives want to give all the money to the oil companies, but exactly the reverse is the case. We are proposing to give all the money to the provinces themselves, reserving for the federal Government the right to impose federal taxes. It is not, therefore, the Crown share itself to which we are opposed, but the execution of the Crown share retroactively without compensation, which is basically unCanadian.
In closing, let me summarize the basic position of the Conservative energy policy which has evolved in discussions and consultations over the last few months. Details of the policy will be announced in the next few weeks but it follows basic principles. First, these include the fact that energy should be used to unite the country, not divide it as the national energy policy has done.
Second, in order to ensure energy security Canada needs balanced development of its energy resources from all regions of the country and from all sources-oil and gas, hydro, nuclear and alternative sources. With adequate resources no region of the country can hold the rest of the nation hostage when it comes to supplies of energy.
Third, it is the responsibility of the federal Government to ensure that the fiscal regime in place will permit the development of the resource in order to create jobs and tax revenues. A punitive tax regime which discourages the development of the resource, as is the case under the NEP, is not in the national interest. I have personally visited Venture and some of the other offshore areas and there is great concern that if the taxation provisions of the NEP are applied, those developments will never go ahead. In fact there is no energy development in the country today, whether Husky Oil in Saskatchewan or the oil sands in Alberta, except where the taxation provisions of the national energy policy have been waived. The national interest is served by an energy policy which allows industry to get on with the job of finding and developing the oil and gas reserves in order to create jobs and revenue and to contribute to a strong and united Canada. That would be the goal of a Conservative energy policy under the Hon. Member for Central Nova.

Entering into a bargaining process with what has served as the federal Government over the last few years is never easy for provincial Premiers. Particularly when Nova Scotia is one of the smaller provinces in Confederation and must deal with that bureaucratic machine in the Department of Energy, it is a tribute to Premier Buchanan that he was able to bargain so effectively and hard on behalf of the people of his province. Having said that, I believe there is a certain amount of nervousness in this Chamber over what we are about to do. In one day we are about to approve a 100-page piece of legislation. It deals with a very complex topic, that of oil and gas.
Let me point out a couple of facts to the House. The Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) entered into an agreement with the Province of Nova Scotia on March 2, 1982. It is June 28, 1984, two years and three months later. For the very first time, elected Members of Parliament are being allowed to consider whether or not that agreement is in the best interest of all Canadians and particularly those who choose to live in the Province of Nova Scotia. When was the first time we saw this legislation? It is dated May 31, 1984. Members of the House first saw it two years and two months after the agreement was reached in private between the Premier and the Prime Minister or his representative.
Members of Parliament have been put into a very awkward position. If one believes in co-operative federalism and good faith bargaining, there is no choice at this late date but to approve a contract that has already been in effect for two years and three months for all practical purposes. That is the dilemma we face today. We must approve the contract because it has existed for a long time and must be legislated in order to take effect. At the same time, however, we look forward to an early election for a change in government and a re-opening of that agreement so that it will make more sense for the future.
I come from the City of Calgary. When I was elected to this Chamber some five years ago we had one of the lowest vacancy rates in the world. We had one of the lowest unemployment rates in the world. We had one of the most aggres-

The then Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, in cooperation with the then Minister of Finance, produced the National Energy Program. It was a bureaucratic nightmare. It took effect as soon as it was produced in budgetary form. The legislation respecting that program was not introduced in the House for quite some time. Members may recall that that omnibus piece of legislation was so onerous and such a denial of the basic principle of free speech and basic common sense that we rang the bells for 17 days.
That was to get that piece of legislation split into manageable parts. That was quite some time after the actual event. We did it with the certain conviction and knowledge that it was a rotten piece of legislation that would be bad for the country. Standing here in June 1984, Mr. Speaker, I can tell you that that Bill is one of the worst pieces of legislation that has ever been inflicted on any nation anywhere in the free civilized world. I am speaking of the National Energy Program. That is what it was and that is what it is.
As a result of the National Energy Program the City of Calgary has seen a lot of suicides and it has a lot of people in mental hospitals. It also has a lot of unemployment. The vacancy rate in office buildings is 25 per cent and for apartment accommodation the vacancy rate is 13 per cent to 14 per cent. The unemployment rate is higher than the national average. These are the circumstances not because the people of Calgary have lost their skills, their desire, or anything else. We have those kinds of conditions because the Liberal Party of Canada in conjunction with the New Democratic Party decided it knew how to run the oil and gas industry. Surely by June 1984 it is self-evident that the Government has no business trying to run that kind of complex industry.
I have a warning for the people of Nova Scotia. Because of the insistence of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) and because of the insistence of the new Leader, Mr. John Turner, who is supporting the Minister of Energy, this House is being seized with Bill C-43 today. We are going to make it law. But the motion before us does not allow the Parliament of Canada, the elected people of this country, to hear witnesses for even five minutes. It will not allow us to hear witnesses for four minutes, for three minutes, for two minutes, for one minute, not even for one second. There are 100 pages of legislation affecting the oil and gas industry. This is surely one of the most technical industries in the world today. It is one of the most competitive industries, and it is one of the really international industries in existence today. But we are not allowed as parliamentarians to take this piece of legislation to committee and to invite knowledgeable people to come before the committee so we can ask them questions and learn whether or not the ideas contained in this Bill are good or bad. That is the Government's choice, Mr. Speaker. That is Mr. Turner's choice. That is the Minister of Energy's choice. They could have arranged the world in a different way. This Party would have welcomed the opportunity to take Bill C-43 to committee. We would have liked to
have had a month or two or three to call witnesses and have them help us examine the clauses.
What is going to happen to the potential jobs and the potential income of the Province of Nova Scotia? There are parts of this Bill that talk about income sharing. The spokesperson on behalf of our Party has indicated that we are in favour of the basic pattern of that income sharing. Surely this nation is waking up to the fact that there can be no sharing without first having some income. The primary obligation that rests on all of us in this Chamber is to arrange the affairs of this nation in such a fashion that wealth is produced. If we do that well, then we have the means to help those who cannot help themselves.
If this is a bad agreement-and I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that there are parts that give all of us much concern-then the people of Nova Scotia will be mightily disappointed. The people of Canada will also be mightily disappointed because that income sharing will not amount to anything. Let me ask you why, Sir. If you were to set out to attract an oil and gas industry to your region, why would you have a provision such as the one found in Clause 90 in this Bill that taxes the industry in that region at a higher rate than it does in other regions? Is that the kind of carrot that will attract an industry? Maybe it will. But that is a federal tax. That is the federal Government laying on an extra 5 per cent tax that is not applicable in other parts of the country.
There is another section in this Bill that deals with definitions and the implications of definitions. I believe that is found in Clause 22, if my memory serves me well. That clause deals with pipelines and with the provision that the Province of Nova Scotia is entitled to the right of first refusal to a 50 per cent ownership position in off-shore pipelines. But if you read the definition of a pipeline as closely and as carefully as you can, may I suggest to the Chair and to the Chamber, to the Premier of Nova Scotia and to the Minister of Energy, that that clause of the Bill is sufficiently unclear that it is very, very likely to end up in the courts.
Is a gas plant a pipeline? If we get an image of a pipeline in our minds we see it going through the ground and we say that this is a pipeline. A gas plant? That is a different kind of structure full of all kinds of pipes with different machines and dials. The definition in this Bill of a pipeline is sufficiently broad, in my view, that the Government of Nova Scotia has the right to first refusal of a 50 per cent ownership position in a gas plant. Is that what was intended by the Premier of Nova Scotia and the Minister of Energy? I suggest it probably was not. I suggest that if this Bill were to be subjected to the normal process that this House, that the parliamentary system, has come to put in place over years and centuries, then we could have testimony as to whether or not we have a definitional problem. If we have, if I am correct in my assessment, we could have suggested some modifications to the clause that would be designed to clear up the discrepancy and make the world a better place.
Having been born in the City of Calgary and lived there about half a century, I have been around the oil and gas
June 28, 1984

industry almost since the first day it came into operation in our region. That is close to 50 years of experience. It is a sensitive industry. It is characterized by mobility. It is a funny industry. At the exploration end of it, it takes money. Money does not respect provincial or national borders. Money is a commodity which travels relatively freely around the world. That is the first thing it takes. Second, it takes committed, dedicated and knowledgeable human beings. They are welcome around the world because they are in short supply. Third, it takes mobile equipment. An oil drilling rig is designed to dig a hole. When the digging is done, it has to be dismantled and moved. If it is on a drilling ship, it simply has to be moved. The characteristic of the required equipment is its mobility.
If we have an agreement which is unsatisfactory to those people who own and control that equipment and to the knowledgeable people who make it work, as well as to those who are willing to take a risk and invest, then it will go. It is mobile. It is easy. It leaves. When it goes, we have increased unemployment, vacancy rates in office buildings and in apartments, increased depression, suicides, heart attacks and spousal battery. Those are the consequences of economic legislation which is badly designed, ineffective and does not work.
We are living through those consequences. Federal politicians in the Liberal Party have forced those of us in the City of Calgary, in the Province of Alberta, to live through those consequences. I do not want that for the people of Nova Scotia. They deserve better. They should have better. Hopefully this agreement will produce better. However, standing in this Chamber on June 28, 1984, all I can say is that it is a hope.
If the Government had chosen to follow a decent process, to allow committee examination and to allow expert witnesses to give testimony, then all of us would have some sense of confidence about what the legislation indicated it would do, what it intended to do. That would have been better for the nation and for the people of Nova Scotia.
I look forward to the day when we have a government which values the process of seeking informed testimony from people in the country before putting in place pieces of legislation which may do a great deal of harm.

Mr. Speaker, I join with my colleagues who preceded me in mentioning again, because it bears mentioning, that this method of passing legislation is really an affront in many ways to the parliamentary system.
Bill C-43 is not a trivial Bill of two or three paragraphs. It is a Bill of 100 pages and some 39 clauses, many of which are technical. It flows from the agreement between the Government of Canada and the Government of Nova Scotia regarding the development of the offshore. As a responsible Party
Canada-Nova Scotia Oil Agreement
and as responsible members of that Party, obviously we do not want to wreck the agreement reached by those two levels of government acting in the best interests of their respective jurisdictions in producing an agreement which would seem reasonable and adequate. On the other hand, there is something fundamentally wrong with that kind of procedure.
Bill C-43 has been brought forward to provide a legal basis for the agreement. After its passage, it will be said that Parliament has acted, Parliament representing the people of Canada, all segments of Canada. However, at no time in this process were the people who must live with the consequences of this law afforded an opportunity to make known their concerns and observations so that we might examine the details of the law in that regard.
The Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) talked about some of the problems with the definitions, for example. I did not hear all his remarks. He may well have mentioned, and probably did mention, the fact that at least six clauses in the Bill allowed ministerial discretion. That sounds like a good thing when we talk in terms of allowing flexibility to accommodate different circumstances, but it also means that there is no certainty as to what are the rules or how to plan. The offshore activities governed by this legislation and this agreement involve the expenditure of many hundreds of millions of dollars, indeed billions of dollars. It is at least unfair, probably unreasonable and very likely damaging to the prospects of investment, to produce a regime which makes it impossible for planners to know precisely what are the rules because they can be changed at any time on ministerial discretion.
We ought to have had the opportunity of examining those clauses and discussing them with the persons who have to live with them-and I am talking about industry people-to find out the consequences on their ability to operate. Will it result in costs being higher? Will it result in their having to employ more lawyers than geologists and engineers to handle the paperwork as opposed to getting on with the job of finding oil and gas?
Any number of questions could be raised. We ought to have had the opportunity to examine them, but we did not. Why? It is because the legislation was not brought forward until this week. Here we are with one day left in the session and the onus is placed upon this Party as to whether or not to allow the agreement to go ahead, with no concern about the fundamental wrongness of proceeding in this manner in the first place. This agreement was signed last year. We ought to have had the legislation debated at second reading months ago, so that we would have had the opportunity in committee, albeit Committee of the Whole, to examine the legislation clause by clause to ensure that it was workable, to ensure that the industry which has to live with it could in fact live with it and that we are not burdening it with excessive regulation, red tape, costs and so on.
It is not just the interest of the people who have to live with it that is involved. There is also the question of the develop-

June 28, 1984
Canada-Nova Scotia Oil Agreement
ment of these very important resources off Nova Scotia around the Sable Island area. That is a very important natural gas find that needs to be developed. With our dollar falling like a stone and interest rates going through the roof, the ability to produce and export that natural gas would have tremendous benefits for our dollar and the interest rates in this country and, needless to say, for the economy of the Maritimes, Nova Scotia in particular, where this development would take place. That is very important.
Because of the way the House Leader and the Government have treated this Parliament in bringing in this Bill at the last moment, we do not have an opportunity to ask those questions. We have to take it on faith that it will work. Frankly, given this Government's record on energy policy, you have to be fairly dense to take anything it produces on faith.
Since 1980, the over-all impact of this Government's energy legislation has been to drive the energy industry into the ground. It has created 25 per cent vacancies in my community of Calgary. Unemployment levels have increased from 3 per cent to 12 per cent and 13 per cent. It has bankrupted thousands and thousands of Calgarians. That has been the effect of this Government's energy program. Therefore, it hurts a lot at this point to pass more energy legislation without detailed examination to ensure that it will not have that effect on the energy sector, albeit the Nova Scotia energy sector this time.
My colleagues, the Hon. Member for Vancouver Centre (Miss Carney) and the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) mentioned this, but I want to mention again the question of the 25 per cent back-in provision of the national energy policy. I do not know that Members opposite appreciate yet just how costly that provision was to Canada, just what it cost us in terms of investment, both Canadian and foreign. I had a conversation with the chief economist of the Conference Board of Canada. He estimated that the National Energy Program in general, and in particular the 25 per cent back-in, cost the Canadian economy S40 billion to $50 billion, representing, generally speaking, about $20 billion of Canadian money that left Canada and $20 billion to $30 billion that did not come here.
Last summer I had the opportunity to spend the day with pension fund managers and other investment managers in Great Britain, in the City of London. We discussed the attractiveness of Canada as an area for them to invest some of their pension funds which they manage. As a rule of thumb, they tried to invest some of their money offshore for risk minimization. Historically, Canada has been a very attractive country in which to place some of that money, along with the United States, Australia and some other countries. However, as a result of the National Energy Program, and in particular the 25 per cent back-in provision which confiscated privately owned property, Canada was no longer looked upon as an attractive area to invest. A democratic country whose Government would authorize and carry through with confiscation of privately owned property without compensation is a country
governed by a Government that cannot be trusted. The atmosphere has changed incredibly.
In about 20 minutes or so, we will hear from the Bank of Canada what is happening to interest rates. We know for sure that they will go up because of the incredible pressure on the dollar. I wonder what might be happening if the National Energy Program and the 25 per cent back-in provision has not been introduced by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) when he was the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources in 1980. There is no doubt that we would not be witnessing this tremendous pressure to the Canadan dollar or this tremendous pressure on increasing interest rates. Incidentally, there would be several tens of thousands of Canadians currently unemployed who would be employed. That is the cost.
The new leader of the Liberal Party, Mr. Turner, apparently intends to cultivate western Canada. He intends to be more open to the west, have a government that is more concerned about the west and have a government that is more responsive to the west. He puts that contention to lie immediately by apparently reappointing the Minister of Finance to that position. The Minister of Finance is the man who single-handedly devastated the economy of western Canada with the National Energy Program. He is being reappointed to the key financial post of the federal Government by a man who says that his objective is to make the west feel a part of Canada.
My suggestion is that if he wants to give my colleague from Calgary West and myself a little concern about our seats in the next election, he ought to make a public statement that under no circumstances will he allow in his government any person associated with the National Energy Program which devastated western Canada. If he made that statement, my colleague and I would have to get back to Calgary and campaign a little harder. However, it does not appear he is going to do that. He is going to reappoint the Minister of Finance, the man who single-handedly destroyed the economy of western Canada. Supposedly this is a new team that will bring the new nirvana. Well, it ain't so.
My colleague from Vancouver Centre went on record as indicating that a Progressive Conservative Government would eliminate the 25 per cent back-in provision. I want to repeat that. It is absolutely the situation. It is very high on the priority list and will occur very quickly when a new Progressive Conservative Government takes over as a signal to Canadians and the rest of the world that the Government of Canada does not confiscate private property but that it respects private property.
Other aspects of the National Energy Program that will be changed are those dealing with the question of the bureaucratic nature of the program which means that to do anything, one needs the approval of seemingly unlimited numbers of bureaucrats on this committee, that committee and the next. The whole program is full of ministerial approvals, which translates into some darn lower level bureaucrat having to approve
June 28, 1984

everything that is being done. The burden of that on any company intererested in exploring and trying to find oil and gas is absolutely horrendous. We have to get away from that.
This Party is determined to get away from that kind of interventionist hands-on bureaucratic red tape approach to an approach of providing adequate incentives, a firm and fair set of rules and instructions so that the doers, the people who are actually going to do something of value for Canada, can go out and do it on the basis of these incentives and rules, as opposed to the current system which says that if you want to do anything, you have to come to Ottawa, get on your knees and beg permission from some bureaucrat to be allowed to do it. That process is marvellous for lobbyists, lawyers and accountants. It does not do a darn thing for the people who are going to try to find the oil and gas this country needs if we are not only to achieve our goal of self-sufficiency and security of supply but also if we are going to get the benefits from this industry which the industry can provide. There is no question that the modest changes a Conservative Government intends to introduce in the beginning will put tens of thousands of Canadians back to work very quickly in this industry alone. There are many more industries about which similar things could be said.
I have one last point to make regarding a concern that goes beyond the energy question to the role of Parliament in our federal system. It is a dilemma for which I do not have the answer. On the one hand there is the question of the responsibility of parliamentarians. What is the role of Members of the House of Commons in the making of law? Do we have a duty and an obligation to examine every piece of legislation that passes through here with the kind of detail necessary so that when we vote approval, we can do so with a clear conscience in the knowledge that this is the best legislation that can be made or that we have at least had the opportunity to make suggestions which may or may not be taken up by the Government? On the other hand, there is the question of the Government of Canada and in this case the Government of Nova Scotia having reached an agreement, and those sovereign Governments having reached that agreement obviously want to get on with it.
This is related to the question of the role federal-provincial conferences play in the governing of this country. If some of the Premiers and the Prime Minister reach an agreement, does that automatically mean that Parliament ceases to have any responsibility or obligation in terms of the effects of that agreement on the jurisdictions for which the Members are responsible? This is not a new problem. It has been with us for some time. I think it is a problem that must be addressed, because I find it very frustrating to stand in the House and look at this Bill which contains 100 clauses of enormous complexity and say in all good conscience that I am confident that this is good legislation and I am prepared to vote in support of all of its details. Apparently I do not have any alternative.

subtopic: CALL FOR INCREASE IN PUBLIC SYSTEM BENEFITS
CALL FOR INCREASE IN PUBLIC SYSTEM BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the failure of Canada's private pension system is obvious from the growing dependence of elderly Canadians on the Canada Pension Plan, the Guaranteed Income Supplement, and additional tax incentives proposed in the February Budget to support private savings.
Over 50 per cent of elderly Canadians are dependent on the Guaranteed Income Supplement and provincial top-ups to support CPP and private plans. Only 54 per cent of working men and 33 per cent of working women have any private pension coverage, leaving the rest dependent on the public pension system for income replacement in retirement. They face a future of poverty unless the public system is designed for adequacy of retirement income. It is presently designed to be inadequate so private plans can flourish.
The Liberal and Conservative response to the inability and unwillingness of private employers to provide pension saving opportunities is to increase tax incentives to private plan holders and virtually ignore coverage for low-income earners by rejecting mandatory pension coverage or increasing CPP benefits and contributions.
To address pension coverage and adequacy for all Canadian workers and their families seriously, we should be striving to reduce the welfare aspect of the public system by increasing the universal Old Age Security to its former prominence, increasing CPP benefits, and adapting credit splitting so that all pensioners may enjoy their own pensions and ensure retirement with security and comfort.

subtopic: FREEDOM OF COMOX CONFERRED ON CANADIAN FORCES BASE

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Hudecki (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: FREEDOM OF COMOX CONFERRED ON CANADIAN FORCES BASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 25, 1984, an historic happening was witnessed in the annals of the Canadian Armed Forces when Mayor George Piercy of Comox, British Columbia, conferred on CFB Comox the freedom of the town at an extraordinary meeting of council. Never before has a Canadian military base with a detachment of U.S.A. military been honoured in this country with the freedom of the town.
On that day the neighbouring city of Courtenay also officially recognized Military Appreciation Week honouring CFB Comox and its squadrons and supporting staff, including its detachment of 50 United States military personnel.
The granting of the "Freedom of the City" by the civilian population to a military formation has its roots deep in history. Its honour pre-supposed very great confidence by the civilian

June 28, 1984
authorities in the integrity, goodwill and discipline of the military base people who live in their community.
It is my concern that the image of a town in the vicinity of a military establishment has been traditionally viewed as a garrison town. This image has now been dispelled. Instead, thanks to the class of soldiers and airmen enlisting in the Canadian and U.S. military today, they form a relationship with their non-military neighbours which goes well beyond the formal affiliation, and has extended to co-operation, mutual support, and friendship.

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO VOLUNTARY WORK OF SERVING OFFICERS
TRIBUTE TO VOLUNTARY WORK OF SERVING OFFICERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a result of the recent debate on the Security Agency, it is apparent that Liberal Members of Parliament are not aware that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police force goes far beyond the call of duty as a law enforcing agency when serving the people of Canada.
For instance, these Members of Parliament apparently are not aware that an officer of the RCMP is the chairman of a committee of interested citizens that has been formed to assist in the prevention of suicide. Several officers of the RCMP are involved with this organization, with Crime Stoppers involving local citizens, and also with the Block Parent Program. They work with young people in the prevention of crime, serving as lecturers in schools and outlining the dangers of getting involved in criminal activities. As well, they assist the Coast Guard and the Red Cross in water safety education programs.
Many people are not aware that in a city the size of Red Deer the RCMP have to deal with approximately 1,400 lost or stolen bicycles in one year. Many youngsters' tears are dried up as a result of returned bicycles.
Members of Parliament should be aware that the RCMP are of great assistance in developing good, safe, and healthy communities in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, last week the Subcommittee on the Taxation of Visual and Performing Artists and Writers issued its report. It stressed fast administrative action on tax problems between Revenue Canada and Canada's artists.
At that time, I suggested, as an urgent matter, that the Minister consider refunds for artists whose files had been re-examined four years into the past. The Minister announced yesterday that he is accepting that recommendation. His Department will initiate tax refunds to those artists who can
be identified. As well, the Department will welcome enquiries from artists in cases where their identity cannot be automatically located.
The other reactions from the Minister are equally sensitive to the arts community. He has considered the subcommittee's ideas carefully and has accepted our major principles. In addition, a conference is scheduled between Revenue Canada and artists' representatives for the autumn. These decisions are welcome news, indeed, to our artists, and are a sincere and substantial beginning to the settlement of these issues.

subtopic: JAPANESE CANADIAN INTERNEES-PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE PARTY POSITION ON COMPENSATION
JAPANESE CANADIAN INTERNEES-PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE PARTY POSITION ON COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, fully 22,000 Japanese Canadians living in British Columbia were forcibly evacuated and interned by the Mackenzie King Government during the 1942-1946 period. Even after the war was over one constituent of mine, whose family had originated in Japan, was required by law to obtain a letter of approval from the Mayor of Calgary before she could move from the Taber area, to which her family had been forcibly moved, to teach in Calgary.
The attitude of the outgoing Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Col-lenette) on this issue must be reprehensible to all thoughtful Canadians. It is my firm conviction that the Mulroney Government will quickly seek an all-Party resolution regretting these events of 1942-1946.
I am delighted that my Leader was quoted in The Globe and Mail on May 16 as indicating his support for a more than symbolic sum of reparation. He said: "I feel very strongly that Canadian citizens whose rights were abused and violated and trampled upon indeed should be compensated". Our Party spokeman on multiculturalism, the Hon Member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta), indicated to one media outlet only yesterday that a Mulroney Government will sit down and negotiate the nature and amount of a fair settlement to Japanese Canadians soon after the coming election.

subtopic: RECIPIENT OF ALBERT EINSTEIN PEACE AWARD
RECIPIENT OF ALBERT EINSTEIN PEACE AWARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some 19 years ago a new phenomenon burst upon the Canadian political scene. In the short span of three years he literally catapulted from Pierre Elliott Trudeau, the iconoclast, to the Right Honourable Pierre Elliott Trudeau, Prime Minister.
June 28, 1984

No period in Canadian history since 1867 has been so eventful and exciting. Through his efforts and leadership Canada moved from the age of puberty to national maturity. While he sometimes infuriated some Canadians and often excited many more of us, he left none of us indifferent. Many times he made us aware that "the folly of mankind is man". He also tried and succeeded in showing us that it need not be so. Of all his great achievements, none demonstrated that more than his final great effort as Prime Minister. I speak, of course, of his mission for world peace, for which he has been awarded the Albert Einstein Peace Award. It is richly deserved!
An era is coming rapidly to an end. It has been an honour and a privilege to have served under his leadership. I know he will continue to speak and work on behalf of Canada and Canadians. When his resignation is accepted by the Governor General on Saturday morning he can leave in the full and confident knowledge that, in parting, he has left very large footprints in the sands of time. "When shall we see his like again?" Thank you, Mr. Prime Minister.

subtopic: CALL FOR WITHDRAWAL FROM INVOLVEMENT WITH COMMERCIAL ENTERPRISES
CALL FOR WITHDRAWAL FROM INVOLVEMENT WITH COMMERCIAL ENTERPRISES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is time that Canada Post started minding its own business. That business, of course, is delivering mail. For the price of a 32-cent postage stamp, taxpayers expect efficient delivery of the mail. That being the case, Canada Post has no right to throw more irons into the fire. The Post Office, it appears, is looking at getting into lotteries, selling insurance, and airline and travel packages. Consumer's Distributing had a brief fling with Canada Post, but it looks like the affair has gone sour.
Is it fair for this gigantic Crown corporation, which is subsidized by the taxpayer, to get involved with activities which will compete with the citizens who subsidize it? I say no, absolutely no. Canada Post and other Crown corporations should not be allowed to use facilities paid for by all taxpayers to have advantages over others.
The public purse has been abused enough, the latest example of which is the baseball pool, which we all know has struck out. It is well known that business and the private sector are able to create jobs at much less expense than Crown corporations or slush funds. Let us have less monkey business and more private business so Canadians can get back to work.
