subsubtopic: WESTERN GRAIN TRANSPORTATION ACT-PROMISE OF INCREASED EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. During the consideration of Bill C-155, the grain transportation legislation, the Government, and this Minister, promised the creation of some 375,000 jobs in Canada. Now, Mr. Speaker, rather than creating jobs, both railways are laying people off in record numbers. System employment in both Canadian National and Canadian Pacific has been reduced by 6,000 people this year over last year. Canadian Pacific, in particular, is currently engaged in a very ruthless program of eliminating operating and maintenance workers in western Canada.
This loss of jobs, Mr. Speaker, and railway investment, constitutes an outright betrayal of the railway workers and the farmers of Canada. What action is the Minister of Transport and his Government taking to ensure that the railways will live up to the commitments made with respect to this legislation? What action has the Government taken to fulfil the promise it made during consideration and debate on that Bill?

subsubtopic: WESTERN GRAIN TRANSPORTATION ACT-PROMISE OF INCREASED EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe the Hon. Member is confusing two different sets of issues. The proposals which were put forward during the course of debate on the Western Grain Stabilization Bill indicated that the change in rates was necessary in order to provide financial leverage to enable the railways to engage in major capital expansion for the railway system in western Canada. Without going into the entire debate, we know that if the investment had not been made there would be a substantial drawback in the ability of that system to deliver grain to our international markets, which is absolutely essential to the health of the economy. I know the Conservative Party has fought against that, but we have always said it was a foolhardy and shortsighted fight, because if we in any way hamper the ability of the transportation system to deliver the goods on time, at efficient prices, then we have totally and completely undermined our international market for grain.
The railways have committed $1.1 billion this year alone into that capital expansion. The Canadian Pacific Railway, as one example, has already started its work on the Rogers Pass tunnel, the largest construction project in North America.
For the Hon. Member to say that there is no work going on and that there is a betrayal, simply shows the Hon. Member does not understand what is happening in western Canada, which is that the railways are engaged in major expansionary programs to expand our transportation system so that we can sell our grain abroad.

subsubtopic: WESTERN GRAIN TRANSPORTATION ACT-PROMISE OF INCREASED EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: If there is any confusion it is in the mind of the Minister. He is obviously being bamboozled by the railroads.

Mr. Speaker, there have been job losses and further lay-offs each and every day. The railways are laying off full-time productive employees, maintenance way workers, B and B workers, railway carmen, electricians and mechanics. In the past two weeks CP issued lay-off notices for another 150 people. It is now estimated that close to 2,000 people in the operating and maintenance trades have been laid off in western Canada. It will be recalled that the Minister proposed a very elaborate advertising program costing some $3.5 million, telling the Canadian people how many job and investment opportunities there were going to be.
Because of this failure to fulfil a promise and commitment, is the Minister prepared to launch a full-scale inquiry to determine why there are job losses rather than job creation? Will he undertake to do that, rather than pussyfoot around with the railways? When will he start treating the workers first rather than the railways, as he suggested in a speech in Toronto recently?

Mr. Speaker, I certainly welcome the new found interest of the Hon. Member in transportation workers. It is too bad he did not show the same interest when he was in this job himself. The fact is we have already referred the matter of railway employment to the Senior Grain Advisory Committee, which was established to bring together all the major participants in the transportation system. The grain producers, elevator companies, railway companies, and unions are all there. That is the place where the issue will be examined. The railways have been asked to demonstrate that they are living up to their commitments. That is the mechanism we put into place to provide all participants in the western grain transportation system with an opportunity for that kind of review and examination.
If the Hon. Member does not believe in that kind of system, if he wants to go around it, if he does not trust the judgment and assessment of all the major participants in the system, it simply shows exactly who is pussyfooting and fooling around.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Energy I will direct my question to the Minister of Finance. He will know that the quickest way to support the Canadian dollar without raising interest rates is to sell more natural gas to the U.S. The Government's decision to stick with a single border price is creating hardship for the West, particularly for natural gas processors in an industry where employment has fallen by 50 per cent. Since a more flexible natural gas pricing system would earn billions of dollars in export sales, help the Canadian dollar, and create new jobs, why does the Government insist on staying with an obsolete pricing system? Is the Minister working with his colleague, the Minister of Energy, to ensure that there is a
Oral Questions
more equitable and economically efficient way of selling our resources?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member should know better. First of all, the price of natural gas was established after extensive consultations with the industry and the producing provinces. The arrangement arrived at represents the point of view of the industry and the provinces concerned, as well as of the federal Government. It was arrived at in agreement with the American authorities.
Obviously the Department of Energy and the Department of Finance are always examining and reviewing the situation, and are open to representations from anyone with views on how we could improve or expand our exports. But surely the Hon. Member cannot assume that just reducing the price would increase the revenue. You might be able to increase sales a little bit, but if you cut the price by half and increase sales volume by only 25 per cent, you end up with less money than you had before, not more. That is not going to help the Canadian dollar, or Canadians. It will only help Americans who would be able to buy Canadian gas at a very cheap rate, without the Canadian industry or people getting more benefits. As a matter of fact they would end up selling their heritage at a lower price than they are getting at the present time, with a lower total revenue. The Hon. lady's recommendation is one that she should examine much further.

The Minister's answer indicates why the Government is so totally out of touch with economic reality. He must be the only person in the country who believes the single border price for natural gas is not obsolete. Everyone else doesn't.

Mr. Speaker, dealing with obsolete taxes and prices, I would like to deal with the Canadian ownership charge imposed by the Government three years ago to pay for Petrofina. That has long since been paid for, yet the Government continues to pile up about $800 million in this account, and another $900 million next year. Since the Government has not brought forward the legislation which will terminate this account, and since Petro-Canada is offering cash discounts amounting to 16 cents a gallon on gasoline, is it the intention of the Government to return this money to the consumer, not through Parliament but through Petro-Canada?

Mr. Speaker, the main obsolete feature in this House certainly has to be the view of the Hon. Member of the situation of natural gas. The price of natural gas was determined in full consultation and with the full agreement of the industry.
Oh, oh!

Is it the Conservative Party's view that they are going to establish this independently of the views of the producers and producing provinces? That is not the view of

this Government, and that is not the policy followed by the Minister of Energy, nor is it the policy we are going to follow. We are going to continue a policy of consultation with the provincial Governments and the industry, and make changes once they have been considered appropriate by all concerned.
As far as the question raised by the Hon. Member is concerned, she knows the tax to which she referred is going to be assigned for energy purposes in Canada, and steps have already been announced in the Budget in that regard.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance. Just about three months ago we had a major increase in interest rates. Then I pointed out to the Minister that we were going through a bad old movie, which has since become a tragic movie in its impact on the people of Canada. The Minister said on March 15: "We have forecast a decline in interest rates between now and the end of the year." I point out that, since he said that, interest rates have gone in one direction and one direction only, that is up. Today they went up by almost a half a percentage point. The 2 per cent increase in interest rates which has taken place in the last 60 days has cost the typical home owner $24,000 on a mortgage. It has cost Canadian business over $2 billion in interest rate cost increases. When is this madness going to stop?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member deplores the increase in interest rates. He will certainly not be alone in that regard. This is generally deplored, not only in Canada but in the developing world and among industrial countries. If he looks at the European countries, or other countries around the world, he will find very serious and strenuous objections to the fact that interest rates are going up at the present time, fundamentally because of what is happening in the United States. For instance, interest rates have gone up a half a percentage point in Austria and Germany in the last day. They have gone up a full point in Sweden, and there are similar increases taking place in a number of other countries. The Hon. Member knows the tragic impact of these developments on developing countries also, and debtor countries in particular.
The issue is obviously related to what is happening in the United States. Strong representations have been made to the Government of the United States by other industrial countries as well as developing countries. We hope that steps will be taken, particularly in the United States, to reverse that particular trend which we all regret and certainly cannot support.

Mr. Speaker, I point out that the people of Canada have some interest in what the Government of the United States is doing in this issue. However, they have
particular interest in the actions of the Government of Canada on interest rates rather than in what other people are doing.

We have made a proposal which we think could be effective in at least curtailing the rate of interest rate increases. The Government discarded that. Farmers, business people, and home owners are suffering. Is it the Government's intention merely to sit back and watch what happens, and allow interest rates to rise to the 20 per cent plus area again, or is the Government going to take some kind of action sometime soon to stop these increases?

Mr. Speaker, we have heard rhetoric rather than proposals from the NDP. I indicated to them that I had examined carefully the suggestion they made, upon which they did not elaborate. I indicated to them that it was filled with counterproductive elements-
Like what?

-which would make it a very ineffective and counterproductive proposal.
With regard to whether we would sit and do nothing, I want to remind my friend that the last time interest rates went up the Government took a number of steps to help farmers and home owners.
What?
Now they ask what. The NDP do not even remember what took place over the last two years.
Bankruptcies, that is what.

I will tell you what is happening now. If you want to buy a house now you can open up a $10,000 RHOSP which is income tax deductible. That means that you can save several thousands of dollars on the purchase of a house at the present time. That program is available at the present time for people who want to buy homes. We have come up with a mortgage interest rate proposal which we had to drag the NDP, kicking and screaming, into approving. That is going to provide support and help for people who have loans at the present time when they must renew their mortgages.
More for the banks.

These are only two among many steps which we have taken. There are a number of programs of the ministry of housing which are helping people at low income levels in terms of social housing. The Hon. Member knows, or should know, that.

Mr. Speaker, I point out to the Minister that it was not only the NDP but the business people involved in the mortgages who pointed out that they could not recommend to the people of Canada the proposal made by the Government. It was totally useless.

Member probably thought I was not in the House, he said that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) had acted improperly and that the Government House Leader was not any good. In the House it is common practice that Ministers with bills to table in the House discuss them with the respective critics in the two Opposition Parties. The Income Tax Act, that's it. The Minister of Finance consulted me yesterday and asked whether he could send a copy of the Bill to his Finance critics on the opposite side of the House. In the circumstances, the Hon. Member is wrong to criticize the Minister of Finance. The Minister is extremely competent and has done wonders at a time when the economy was in great difficulty. easily influenced and has remained very close to the people and to the Members of the Opposition, and that he decided to trust them and submit bills to them prior to tabling them in the House, something he did again only recently.

Member, who is Parliamentary House Leader for the Progressive Conservative Party (Mr. Hnatyshyn) will have a chance to agree on a limited debate tomorrow to adopt this Bill. speechtext:
that Bill C-248, an Act to amend the Public Service Employment Act and the Public Service Staff Relations Act (political rights), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is the umpteenth time that a Bill of this nature has been presented in Parliament since the 1950s. However, the last time this occurred was on April 30, 1982, at which time Members from all sides of the House agreed with the Bill, but there was no agreement for it to be passed. At this time I called as my witness the late lamented and departed Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton who spoke in favour of this Bill and urged that it be passed. I want to remind Hon. Members, Mr. Speaker, that a gentleman by the name of Guy D'Avignon was Chairman of the special committee appointed by the Government to review personnel management, conditions of employment, the merit principle and other aspects of the Public Service. I would like to read to the House the first paragraph of his report, which reads as follows:
Citizens of a democracy have a right to take an active part in the political process; by their actions they assure a healthy, responsive democratic system of government. Today, no one would lightly propose the extinction of this right with regard to any individual or group.
But the Government chose to ingore that part of the report having to do with political rights. The report was made, by the way, in the spring of 1979. The Chairman of the committee recommended that public servants be put in three categories when it came to political rights. The third category would cover probably 85 per cent or 90 per cent of the federal Government and Crown corporation employees.
Just two or three weeks ago, Mr. Speaker, we witnessed a situation where rank and file federal public civil servants elected as delegates to a national convention of a Canadian political Party were threatened with dismissal, or will be dismissed, because on their own time they took part, as can any other citizen, in the political process. One of those delegates comes from the City of Winnipeg. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) said it was a little bit of a denial of their rights but that it is the Public Service which makes the rules. The Public Service Commission makes rules, Mr. Speaker, based upon the legislation, and until we change the legislation, the Public Service Commission cannot change the rules.
I want to remind Hon. Members that in the experience of the United Kingdom, which has, one has to concede, a professional public service, that public service has had full political rights for many years. Whether or not it chooses to exercise those rights is entirely its own decision. Many public servants do, some do not.
My Bill, Sir, would exclude those who are in what one could call the "Order in Council category". They could still exercise their political rights because they have a contractual arrangement with the Government, with the Cabinet, whether it be a Deputy Minister or the head of a board or whatever. They can still choose to be politically active and would know ahead of time that they were taking their chances as to their reappointment. However, Sir, that does not apply to the tens of thousands of clerks and stenographers, people in many categories of employment in the Public Service.
In 1945, the Government of Saskatchewan under Tommy Douglas not only provided for the right to organize, the right to bargain collectively, but also the right to take part in political activity. Once and for all we removed the ability of a government of any political strijpe to prohibit or inhibit any public servant or Crown corporation employee in Saskatchewan from taking part in the political process if they chose to do so. Four other provinces have done the same thing. However, this place, which should have been setting the example and leading the way, has not done so.
I can cite my own experience, Mr. Speaker, as an employee of Canadian Pacific Limited. You will agree, Sir, that there was not much love lost between my Party and the CPR in terms of what we considered bad corporate behaviour on its part for a hundred years or more. However I felt then from 8.30 in the morning until 5.30 in the afternoon, at no time did
June 28, 1984

I say or do anything of a political partisan nature when I was on duty and being paid by the company which employed me. I did all I could in as conscientious a manner as I could to earn the salary I was being paid for conducting the company's business. However, after 5.30 in the afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I went to political meetings. I obtained leaves of absence to work as an organizer, to be a candidate, and I returned to my job without any loss of seniority. It ended up, Mr. Speaker, that that corporation and I severed relationship, at my decision. I resigned. But for all the years I worked for that corporation I was able to participate in the political process on my own time, on leave of absence without pay or on holidays with pay.
Surely, Sir, we cannot allow that right for some groups and not for others. We must allow that right for all. Some day, and I am surprised it has not happened yet, some federal public servant is going to take the Government of the day to court and will win. Why should we wait around asking for that kind of trouble?
My Bill provides for deletion of Section 39(2) of the Public Service Staff Relations Act which would mean, Sir, that the organization to which the federal public servants belong could use the dues which were paid to it in any manner it sees fit, including contributions to a political Party or a candidate of a political Party. Again, Sir, other organizations in other parts of our economy are able to do this, whether it is a trade union, business association, or any other kind of organization. The members of the organization themselves decide how much they will pay in the way of dues and how they will spend those dues, and that is perfectly proper. If a chamber of commerce, a business organization, a trade union or a farm organization decides it wants to expend some of its own funds, a decision agreed to by its members, on behalf of or opposed to any political Party or candidate, it can do so and in fact it does so now. It has the right to do so.
That is a minor part of my Bill, Mr. Speaker. If the Public Service employees of the federal Government were to decide by a democratic vote that they wanted to spend their money on behalf of a Conservative, a Liberal or an NDP candidate, or any political Party, or if they wanted to spend some money against that Party, they should be able to do so as well as anyone else. That is only a minor provision of the Bill compared to what I and others before me are trying to accomplish. We have to recognize that employees of the federal Government, including the House of Commons, taking part in the political process while off duty do not harm the Government of the day or Parliament. Experience in several provinces here and in the United Kingdom has shown that any time public employees have participated in a political process, no matter what their success or otherwise, they returned to their duties and carried them out in a conscientious and trustworthy manner. That certainly was our experience in Saskatchewan. We had provincial civil servants who ran as candidates for the Social Credit, Conservatives, Liberals and New Democrats. Some of them won, some did not. The ones that did not, returned to their duties. We even had former members of the legislature from different Parties who kept their positions in
Political Rights
the employ of the government long after they were members of the legislature, even when the government changed. To their credit, they all carried out their duties in a conscientious manner.
We are no longer in the days of patronage when federal public servants had no bargaining rights. They were all hired and fired by the government in power. A government in power can no longer do that. These people have their own organization and the right to bargain collectively. Those rights include their political rights.
Since the House has been in such an amenable mood these last few days, and since we just passed two Bills in Private Members' Hour by unanimous consent through all stages, I would like to ask the House to do the same thing in this instance. I have spoken to Members on all sides and I would like to obtain agreement that we pass this Bill through all stages so that it becomes the law of the land before the next federal election. Tens of thousands of federal public servants have been told by Members of all political Parties, publicly and privately, that they should have the same political rights as others. This is an excellent opportunity for all Members in this House to put their actions where their mouths are. I hope my good friends in the Conservative and Liberal Parties will rise in their places for five or ten minutes, if they want to speak on this Bill, but not talk it out. I hope they will support what our former colleague, the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton, had to say on this Bill in 1982. We have had two years to think about it. Surely it is time to provide federal public servants with the same political rights that the rest of us enjoy. Democracy is indivisible; you cannot divide our people into groups, one of which can go to a meeting but another which cannot. Surely it is time, particularly given our new Constitution, to put an end to this treatment of federal public servants. I hope that my colleagues on all sides of the House agree that we can put this Bill through in all stages today.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) has certainly put forward an interesting proposition this afternoon. Bill C-248 relates to political activity by public servants and amends the Public Service Employment Act and the Public Service Staff Relations Act concerning political activity. It is my understanding that the present Act provides for limited activity such as party membership, the ability to attend certain Party meetings and so on, but it does not provide for high profile political activity or senior positions in political Parties. The Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections has been studying for the last few days matters relating to the ability of people to become candidates in election campaigns and so on. The Hon. Member has made the argument about how the Bill of Rights grants certain political rights in this country. Obviously he firmly believes that we should change the historical nature of our Public Service from one that is politically neutral to one which is politically active.

June 28, 1984
Political Rights
I think of the Jacksonian democracy in the United States. I believe it was Andrew Jackson in the U.S. election campaign of 1820 who said that to the victors go the spoils. That of course is a very important part of the U.S. democratic system, but it is quite different here in Canada. I think the Public Service generally, certainly at the federal level, has operated very well on a neutral basis. In fact, there are very strict rules about Party activity.
I appreciate the arguments the Hon. Member makes, and if you looked strictly at the Charter of Rights I guess you would agree with his arguments. On the other hand, I think we have to look at it from the public's perception of how the Public Service operates. It is perceived to be neutral? The Hon. Member outlined how he was able to be completely neutral in the daytime and be a Party activist in the hours off work. I am interested in those comments because I noted that when the Government introduced in the House what was to become the 1967 Public Service Staff Relations Act, it had been subjected to further scrutiny and consultation on the part of interested parties. When the matter was before the special joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons concerning the public service the late David Lewis said that it may perhaps surprise members of the committee to hear that he was in favour of organizations of public servants being prohibited from acting on behalf of a political Party. Whatever the case may be with other employee organizations, Mr. Lewis said that he did not think you could have a public service organization affiliated with or working on behalf of any political Party.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE EMPLOYMENT ACT PUBLIC SERVICE STAFF RELATIONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: That is not the point.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE EMPLOYMENT ACT PUBLIC SERVICE STAFF RELATIONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
The public perception of the public service is very important in this regard. Senior executives have been prohibited from becoming candidates in election campaigns because it is felt that they have a senior managerial or executive role. Staffing officers have been prohibited under Section 32 of the Public Service Act because it is felt that if they were perceived to be partisan and people got turned down for jobs that would adversely reflect on the public service. Officers enforcing regulations have not been permitted extensive political activity because when they are enforcing regulations and laws it is felt that it is important that they be perceived to be completely neutral and impartial.
Page 36 of the report of the Special Committee on Personnel Management and The Merit Principle reads as follows:
With respect to public servants who perform a regulatory role, many interven-ors stated that these public servants should not be given freedom to participate in Party politics. Otherwise, the public might well perceive that a licence denial had political connotations when, in fact, it stemmed from failure to meet the requirements for granting of a licence. The theme of most intervenors who took this position was that, when public servants are in direct contact with the general public, they must be seen to be politically neutral. The possibility of meeting a public servant during the day as a regulator of Government policy and meeting him again at night as a campaign worker for a political Party could be damaging to the credibility of the public service. Examples of employees in this category were given as: radio inspectors, customs officials, CEIC officers, and fisheries inspectors.
I think it is good that this issue be debated. Times are changing and nothing is cast in stone for all time. People are more active politically and want to be so. The Charter of Rights suggests that these are principles of freedom of expression and association which are important. I think that we have been generally served by a public service which has been able to act impartially and be perceived to be impartial to political partisan association. Before we change that we should make sure that any new directions would be perceived by the general public to be better. 1 think it is good that we debate this issue from time to time. However, I personally would not recommend making the changes which the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) is proposing to us this afternoon.

This gentleman, who happens to live in my constituency, was dismissed by the senior officers of Canada Post because they alleged that he had a conflict of interest. If this Bill in its present form were to have been in place and extended, as it should be, to Crown corporations, Mr. Varma would still be serving as an employee of Canada Post and discharging duties in the fashion that he has for the benefit of the taxpayers of the country.
Mr. Varma came to two Members of our Party, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) and the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), having been frustrated in his endeavours to convince senior officials of that corporation, which is the successor of a Government Department, that there were some unusual occurrences within the Department which were not remedied when that Department became a Crown corporations. In particular, Mr. Varma indicated that he was hired to assist in a managerial position with respect to computer programs. He indicated that it was very strange to find, despite the fact that the corporation had acquired expensive pieces of computer equipment, that the equipment was set aside and replaced with a system acquired as a consequence of the recommendation of certain senior officials of the Post Office Department, as it then was. Upon investigation, it appears that those senior officials had a vested interest in the company supplying those services. I am not talking about small, non-consequential amounts of money. There was some $3 million involved in that little project.
He tried to convince other officers of the Department that there was something amiss with the equipment that they then
June 28, 1984

had and which was developed internally, in that the equipment broke down with some surprising regularity. Such regularity smacked of sabotage. There happened to be two sets of this equipment operating in two separate locations. It was only the set in the location where the senior officer had an indirect interest with the supplier of the new product that the product on site continued to break down.
Matters became so serious that the RCMP was called in to investigate the circumstances surrounding both the breakdown in the equipment and the supply of the new equipment, and whether or not there was in fact a conflict of interest. The conflict of interest should be given its proper name, that is corruption. The RCMP investigation has never been made public and the officials of Canada Post today allege that to make that information public would reflect badly on both officials within Canada Post and people with whom Canada Post has business dealings.
As a consequence of the release of this information by this honest, public spirited citizen, the Auditor General has undertaken a complete investigation of the activities of this bloated Crown corporation to determine whether the charges made by Mr. Varma are accurate.
It is interesting to note that this man, while hired at a senior post, resigned that position to take a position as a postal clerk. He then agreed that in the event that his charges were not substantiated he would cheerfully resign. He was approached and intimidated by officers and finally fired by a man named Mr. Bodrug in the Toronto office of Canada Post. Mr. Bodrug is a man who I have endeavoured on numerous occasions to reach by telephone to deal with this problem and others that have concerned my constituents. This pompous potentate, who believes that he is above all other authority and beyond the realm of the House, has absolutely refused not only to return my telephone calls but to even speak to me. The message that he has left is that he will not have any conversations with me at all. This is the man who fired Mr. Varma.
Mr. Varma is the man who has gone to the extent that he has jeopardized his livelihood for the sake of assisting the people of Canada in getting a fair and honest deal from suppliers to Canada Post. He is fired and Bodrug is there, the man who dismissed him. Of course, Bodrug will not have any conversations with Members of Parliament. However, they have appointed an official who will have conversations with us, but this official has no authority to either say or do anything. That has become so typical of the way in which Crown corporations and government departments function.
These public servants are not asking for a reward, they are simply asking that some justice be done because there is some chicanery taking place. I believe very clearly that in the event public spirited public servants cannot, within the realm of their own departmental or Crown corporation function, convince their superiors that something is amiss, and if they cannot get a fair hearing to unearth the trouble, they are surely entitled to go to the only place where there should be people interested in

Mr. Speaker, I too would first like to commend the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) for bringing the Bill before the House. I also have concerns about the Bill. I will not speak long so that other members will have an opportunity to speak.
I suggest that there are two problems with the Bill. The first problem is clearly that which was pointed out by the Hon. Member for York North (Mr. Gamble). I think it is blatantly obvious why that particular clause was put in the Bill by the Hon. Member for Regina West.
Second, and we have discussed this at length in the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates with the Chairman of the Public Service Commission, others and my constituents, the Bill is too broad. It is precisely what I said when we debated this Bill two years ago when the late Hon. Member for Nepean Carleton was here and made a contribution. If my memory serves me correctly, he agreed with me that the Bill as it is drafted is too broad.
A separation has to be made in this legislation in defining political rights. This is not the case now. They are not well defined. It is a very vague situation that public servants face. But the differentiation has to be between those people who are involved in policy, who interact on a regular basis with a minister, which goes far beyond the deputy head who is the only person excluded by the Hon. Member's Bill. It has to separate those involved in direct dealings with the Minister in a policy aspect and those who are not. Those who are not involved in direct policy dealings with a Minister should not be restricted in their political activities. I do not know how many times we have to say this among ourselves before it finally gets through, but that is the way the law should read. Those involved in policy who are meeting with a minister on a regular basis should refrain from overt political activity. It is obvious why. If Governments change, it can place the jobs of those senior people in the bureaucracy in jeopardy.
The Hon. Member for Regina West knows very well what happened to identified New Democrats in the Province of Saskatchewan when Mr. Devine's government came to power. Those people under Saskatchewan legislation at the senior level were allowed to politicize themselves. They did. When Mr. Devine's government came into power he swept them out of their jobs.
We want continuity in the Public Service. It is important to have continuity. The way you can combine the notion of continuity in the Public Service with the freedom to have political activity is to separate that notion on the basis of policy. Those people who interact with ministers and those people who have a policy impact should be precluded from overt political activity. Those people who do not should be free to have political activity. But the Bill before us is too broad. It says only deputy heads, and order-in-council appointments cannot involve themselves in political activity or politicize themselves. That is where the Bill goes wrong. Again, it is still wrong. Two years ago I said to the Hon. Member, and I say it again, if he brought forward a Bill that took that into consideration I could certainly stand in this place today and support it.
We have laws in place now. Section 32 of the Public Service Employment Act says that a public servant cannot participate on behalf of a candidate or a political party during an election. And then there was some misconstrued interpretation, according to me, and I am on the record in the Standing Committee on Public Accounts when Mr. Gallant, the Chairman of the Public Service Commission was before the committee. The misconstrued interpretation of the Public Service Commission was that somehow that applies to all cases of political activity
June 28, 1984

by public servants. Through the use of Section 7 of the Financial Administration Act, which allows the deputy head to take disciplinary action, notes and memos were sent out to every public servant prior to the Liberal leadership convention indicating that no public servant could involve himself or herself in any way in the leadership convention.
There are some other problems, Mr. Speaker. The Act allows individuals to be members of political parties and to attend political meetings, make contributions to political parties, but a person cannot work on behalf of a candidate during the period of an election. We have to make this clear.
What if, for example, a person wants to run in an election. That is precluded by the Public Service Employment Act. A public servant may not stand for election to federal office, to provincial office, or to territorial office. But a public servant may, if he or she gets leave of absence from the Public Service Commission. You apply for leave of absence from the Public Service Commission, as I did when I was a public servant. I was denied. The person who ran against me for the New Democratic Party works in the National Archives. That person applied for leave of absence and he was granted leave of absence. When he was defeated in my riding he went back to the National Archives.
What criteria did the Public Service Commission use? It used precisely the criteria I am describing today. Does this person have a policy input? Does this person interact with a minister? Yes, he does. No, he may not have a leave of absence. No, he does not. Yes, he may have a leave of absence. The law the way it stands now in this particular case is an ass. It is ridiculous.

The leave of absence is clearly given so a person can express openly and plainly, so the world can see, political affiliation, political partisanship. But the person has to do it off the job so to speak.
What is the purpose of the law? The purpose according to the Chairman of the Public Service Commission, in discussions I have had with him, is that public servants' political leanings should be veiled so the public does not get the feeling that there is a partisan aspect to the service of the public. How can you possibly say that there is a veil before the partisanship of a public servant when you have just granted that person a leave of absence, he or she has gone through an eight-week campaign, having his or her name plastered all over the riding and then the individual comes back to work afterward, having lost. You now say: "The veil goes back up again. You really did not see that person campaigning."
The criteria are so loose and the provisions are so vague that public servants do not know what is possible, what is allowable, what is not allowable, or what is fair or what is not fair. The situation we have now is not fair. It is not clear, it is not just, and there is no way that we should be trying to administer a law that allows a bureaucracy to arbitrarily decide what is and what is not appropriate behaviour in the workplace on the basis of guidelines that do not exist.
