June 28, 1984
Bank Act

Mr. Speaker, since the Bank Act revisions of 1980, which allowed for the first time foreign bank subsidiaries to become Canadian chartered banks, nearly 60 foreign bank subsidiaries have been incorporated as full members of the Canadian banking community. Under the terms of the 1980 Bank Act, foreign bank subsidiaries are limited to 8 per cent of the total domestic assets of the banking system. The legislation now before the House would raise the domestic asset ceiling on the foreign bank section to 16 per cent.
Experience suggests that the foreign bank subsidiaries have benefited Canadians in a variety of ways, including the provision of a competitive source of medium-size business financing, promotion of export activities and the creation of new employment opportunities. Moreover, the foreign bank sector as a whole is responsible for a substantial inflow of new capital into the Canadian economy. I would add that this is a matter of some urgency since some of the foreign bank subsidiaries now benefiting borrowers are already constrained in their ability to make additional loans.
It has long been a policy of the Government to increase competition in the banking industry. This reflects the fact that a handful of major banks control an overwhelming share of the domestic banking market. Accordingly, the 1980 Bank Act made provision for the entry of foreign bank subsidiaries as a way to increase competition. At the same time, however, the Government was conscious of a need to ensure that control be maintained in such an important sector. As a result, the foreign bank subsidiaries were limited in their share of the domestic market. The 8 per cent domestic asset ceiling is enforced by provisions in the Bank Act that limit the total domestic assets of each subsidiary of a foreign bank to 20 times the deemed authorized capital distributed by the Minister of Finance.
We are a trading nation, dependent to a large degree upon international trade and capital flows for our prosperity. The fact that Canada's largest chartered banks are active internationally is a reflection of that basic fact. The presence of Canadian financial institutions in foreign markets benefits Canadian exporters and serves as an efficient conduit for the international flow of funds. Since Canada has a comparatively small capital market, we require foreign funds to assist us in developing our abundant wealth of natural resources and to create jobs. However, the fact that our domestic banks are active in foreign markets results in demands for reciprocity by foreign Governments. Consequently, the Government feels that it would be advantageous to our long-term interests to ensure that Canadian banks remain active in foreign markets. The measure now before the House will assist in achieving that goal.
When the 8 per cent domestic asset ceiling was implemented, it was envisaged that as the domestic assets of the Canadian banks grew, so too could the domestic assets of the foreign bank subsidiaries. That is, the foreign banks would expand their asset bases, but because the banking system as a whole
would be growing, the 8 per cent ceiling would be maintained. However, in late 1982, the banking system began to contract as personal and business borrowers repaid bank debt. Consequently, while foreign bank subsidiaries applied for and were granted increases in their deemed authorized capital as they neared their individual lending limits, there was an increasing risk that the 8 per cent domestic asset ceiling would be reached. As a result, the issue of the domestic asset ceiling and the status of the foreign bank subsidiaries was referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
The report that was prepared by that Standing Committee was tabled last autumn. It contained a number of unanimous recommendations including a recommendation that the domestic asset ceiling be removed completely. The committee also proposed that the Government undertake a review of all financial institutions. I am pleased to say that this process is already well under way. However, the foreign bank sector remains constrained by the 8 per cent domestic asset ceiling.
In making its recommendation that the ceiling be lifted, the Standing Committee noted that foreign bank subsidiaries have greatly contributed to the development of more competitive practices. This view was voiced by most witnesses who appeared before the committee. In addition, the committee found that the foreign bank subsidiaries have been a source of innovative financing practices and an important catalyst for change. Further, the evidence clearly indicates that the foreign bank sector has become an important and competitive source of funds for medium-sized businesses.
Since the Government's objective in introducing foreign bank subsidiaries into Canada was to promote competition, I am gratified that the committee determined that this goal has been met. As I have noted, the Government's policy is to encourage competition in the banking system. All the available evidence suggests that raising the domestic asset ceiling would benefit Canadians by providing a greater level of competition.
It should be pointed out that some Members are concerned that Canadian non-bank financial institutions are not getting a fair deal from the Government. I can assure them, however, that this is not the case. I have personally been in contact with representatives of such institutions and have held useful discussions with them. Moreover, at the beginning of this year, I established a private-sector advisory committee to assist me in identifying potential policy problems inherent in the changing structure of the financial services industry and examining proposals for change to non-bank financial institution legislation.
The convening of this committee underlines the fact that the Government has no intention of embarking on an ad hoc program of legislative change. Rather, it seeks to formulate a reasoned, well balanced approach to important public policy issues. I should like to point out that the Standing Committee explicitly recommended that this review process be undertaken. This has now been done. It is now our intention to respond to the main concern raised by the committee, namely, that the foreign bank subsidiaries be given the opportunity to expand.



June 28, 1984

The Government's decision to raise rather than remove entirely the domestic asset ceiling reflects the fact that the removal of the ceiling would involve important questions of principle that should be considered in the context of a broader review of financial institution legislation including the decennial Bank Act review. At the same time, however, raising the ceiling to 16 per cent will provide the foreign bank sector with the additional room to expand and to continue serving Canadian borrowers in a manner consistent with the original intent of the Government.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would ask the House to consider the following facts. First, foreign bank subsidiaries have contributed to the introduction of more competitive banking practices, particularly by providing services to medium-sized businesses. This was the guiding principle which lay behind the 1980 Bank Act revisions. Second, the all-Party Standing Committee unanimously recommended that the domestic asset ceiling be removed completely. Third, while the Government endorses the view that foreign banks have made the Canadian banking system more competitive, the retention of a market share restriction will ensure that Canadian control of the financial system will not be gradually eroded. Finally, the Government has been responsive to the concerns of nonbank financial institutions. The review process now being conducted by my committee will assist us in ensuring that the process of legislative change is conducted in a rational and orderly manner.
It is the Government's view that Bill C-30 will enable the foreign bank sector to continue to serve Canadian borrowers and that Canadians have reason to expect to benefit from its passage. A larger foreign bank sector will make our banking sector less concentrated and should contribute to a business environment more conducive to small and medium-sized enterprises.

Mr. Speaker, after listening to the rosy prediction just read by the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. MacLaren), it seems that there is no doubt that this Bill should pass, if we are to believe all that we have heard. I have some serious doubts about the comments that were made, however.
For instance, the Minister said that Canada's control of the banking system will not be gradually eroded. In 1980, four years ago, the maximum amount of domestic asset holdings by foreign banking institutions in Canada was 8 per cent. Four years later, it will double to 16 per cent under this Bill. Is that gradual erosion or is that rapid erosion? Did the Minister really say that Canadian control of the banking institutions in this country would not be gradually eroded but would be rapidly eroded? Is there any significance to Canadian control of the banking institutions in this country? If there is, then I think the Government might well look at what it is doing.
There are a number of things about this Bill that bother me. Indeed, in his rather lengthy written speech, the Minister made no reference to those things at all. I am troubled by the fact that the chief reasons for the amendments to the Bank Act of 1980 that was given to the House and the country was
Bank Act
that it would permit Canadian banks to engage in activities worldwide. It was indeed a measure of reciprocity. Canadian banks were becoming international with head offices in Canada. If that is the case, where are the reciprocity clauses? We know, for instance, that Canadian banks cannot engage in banking activities in France because the French Government has nationalized the banks in France. Unless our banks wish to become nationalized, they cannot engage in banking activities in that country. Why then are French banks entitled to engage in banking activities in Canada?
I know what the Minister would say in answer to that. He would say that he heard evidence from those who appeared before the Finance Committee indicating that the emergence of foreign banking activities in Canada has created greater competition and the customers of Canadian banks have all benefited from that. I was not present at the hearings of the Standing Committee on Finance. That evidence may indeed have been offered. I do not doubt it for a moment.
However, I will say that there has been in large measure an attraction of foreign banks, carrying on activities in Canada, to the subsidiary businesses of foreign corporations that operate in Canada. Some of these corporations are large and very profitable and the banking profits that can be generated from them would be an asset to the Canadian banking institutions. By and large there has been an attraction, as I have indicated, and a siphoning off of that very profitable banking business which was formerly done exclusive by Canadian banks. It is now done by foreign banks which, through their parent operations in foreign nations, act for the parents of the Canadian subsidiary customers.
There is a matter which has been drawn to our attention which should be dealt with before this Bill is passed. The matter concerns an action by a foreign justice department against a Canadian bank. I am talking, of course, about the U.S. Justice Department and the bank is the Bank of Nova Scotia. Members will know that as a consequence of an investigation into organized crime, the United States Justice Department went to its Grand Jury with evidence that ultimately gave rise to the issuing of subpoenas for material which was in the hands of a U.S. branch of the Bank of Nova Scotia. That branch had been used by a customer to dispatch funds to another branch of the Bank of Nova Scotia in the Cayman Islands. The suspicion of the U.S. Department of Justice was to the effect that the funds were derived as a consequence of illegal activities in the United States and, more particularly, the offensive and horrendous drug trade activities in the U.S.
The laws of Cayman would apparently preclude the release of information which was in the hands of the Bank of Nova Scotia through its branch on the island. The U.S. Justice Department employed the tactic of pressuring the Bank of Nova Scotia, through its U.S. branch, to provide information to it which it did not have at its disposal and could only obtain through the branch in the Cayman Islands.

June 28, 1984
Bank Act
In order to obtain that information in a third jurisdiction, it was necessary to approach the Government of the Cayman Islands with evidence of the illegal nature of the activities which gave rise to the transfer of those funds. The U.S. Justice Department refused to do so and its officials said that under their laws, because the issue had first been presented to the Grand Jury, it was contrary to the rules of evidence to admit to the scrutiny of a foreign country the nature of the evidence before the Grand Jury had ruled on it. That is all very well. It would then appear in law that the U.S. Justice Department was precluded from exercising its ordinary rights to obtain that vital piece of information from the Cayman Islands.
However, they decided to proceed in a devious fashion. They decided that they would oblige the Bank of Nova Scotia to release the information to them on penalty of a substantial daily fine. Of course, that fine would ultimately be paid out of the revenues of the bank. They are asking a Canadian bank to breach the laws of confidentiality in a third foreign country on penalty of a substantial fine every day that the information is not made available. It has made a determined effort not to follow the normal course that is available to the U.S. Justice Department of going to the Government of Cayman and releasing the information, which would then give rise to a proper release of whatever information the branch of the Bank of Nova Scotia happens to have on the Cayman Islands.
The U.S. Government has made a mistake and it is trying to make a Canadian bank pay for it. I believe that that kind of issue should have been resolved before this Bill was brought before the House. We rarely get an opportunity to have any direct influence from this House of Commons on the way in which our nationals, be they individuals or corporations, are treated in foreign countries. The Government allegedly looks after Canadian citizens and corporations. Sometimes it does that in a rather slipshod fashion. It is in this House that we might well have delayed the passage of this Bill until we had an undertaking by the U.S. Government to proceed in the proper fashion and not badger and fine excessively a Canadian banking corporation which, if it follows the demands which have been made upon it, will be subject to criminal proceedings in a third country.
In making these comments, under no circumstances do I wish anyone to interpret my remarks as being some kind of condonation or protection for illegal activities. However, there is a way to obtain the information in a very proper legal fashion. Certain governments fail to take the steps required in order to obtain what they say they need and then use the clout of a fine against a Canadian bank to get indirectly what they cannot obtain directly. It should have been the duty of this House and its Members to speak out with respect to this issue before the Bill was brought before the House. I regret the fact that that has not been done.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have an opportunity to say a few words about Bill C-30, and Act to amend the Bank Act, particularly when we consider that Canadian home owners today are being driven to the wall, that the Canadian farming sector is
experiencing probably the most difficult time since the 1930s, and that the small business sector is debating whether it is time to walk away from its operations and declare receivership or bankruptcy.
It is a very tough situation. Canadians are expecting action from this Government on a regular basis. That action is not forthcoming. However, there are certain groups which are receiving some attention by this Government. We are discussing one of those groups at the moment-the foreign banks which operate in Canada.
Almost 60 foreign banks have asked for a very special concession. They have said that we ought to break with tradtion and freeze the Bank Act in this country for ten years in order to bring some stability into the banking system of Canada. The foreign banks have asked the Government to change this precedent. They have asked for a special concession. The 58 foreign banks from Japan, Korea, Israel, Greece and France which are operating in Canada, want a special concession from the Government. The Government is allowing that special concession.
The Government is ignoring Canadian small businesses. It is ignoring the fishing sector, the forest sector and the mortgage holders of Canada. The Government is ignoring the average Canadian individual who wants to borrow from the bank. However, when it comes to foreign banks, the Government feels that they ought to receive special treatment. That is what Bill C-30 gives-special treatment to the handful of foreign banks which are operating in Canada. I think it is a very black day when the Government considers this to be a priority item. It brings this legislation forward in the closing minutes of this Parliament. The Government considers this to be a priority item and it wants the House to pass this particular Bill. The assumption was, in terms of the government's explanation, that these banks provide a great deal of competition. Having 58 foreign banks operating in Canada with a greater amount of flexibility in terms of their banking operations, and with more of the banking action available to them, the Government says is going to help the small business people. But when one looks at the facts, they indicate something totally different.
The foreign banks have come into this country, almost falling over themselves, since 1980, getting into position to cream off the corporate loans of Canada. After all, when one considers that the overwhelming majority of these banks are located in three cities, Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver, and the overwhelming majority of them is in one single province, and when one considers that for all intents and purposes there are no branch offices at all, one cannot help but see that it is impossible for the foreign banks in their present state to offer much of a service to the small business sector and to the consumers of Canada. Yet these banks say, "Oh, yes, we are interested in helping the small borrower". However, when one looks at the size of their loan portfolios, one finds that loans in the $5 million to $25 million range account for 44 per cent of the foreign banking action, whereas with respect to domestic
June 28, 1984

banks, only 16 per cent of their total banking action are the $5 million to $25 million accounts. What about the loans under $1 million? The foreign banks have 6 per cent in that particular category, whereas the domestic banks have 28 per cent. It is perfectly clear from the data available, Mr. Speaker, that the service to the small business sector is simply not there. Of the assets of foreign banks, 70 per cent has been loaned to corporations with yearly revenues in excess of $80 million. This is not where we need help today, Mr. Speaker. This is not the sector which requires special consideration. We are saying that if the foreign banks want to expand their operations in this country, if they want special consideration in order to benefit themselves, they ought to indicate a little more clearly that they are here to assist those people who need help these days, namely, the consumers and the small business sector.
Out of the House of Commons report on foreign banks came a set of eight recommendations. It was agreed upon by the Finance Committee that some changes ought to be required, but the Government chose to focus on only a single recommendation. We have not not heard clearly about the whole set of other recommendations which came out of that particular analysis, Mr. Speaker. Quite frankly, I feel it is a little arrogant of the Government to say, "This is the kind of approach we are going to take. We are going to ignore seven recommendations out of eight and, by and large, focus on the one which is going to provide special assistance to the foreign bank". The institutions most likely to be hurt by this Bill are going to be the small Canadian owned banks which are today struggling against the oligopolistic role which the "big five" have in our country, and one can see that they are also going to to be up against the 19 American banks, the two Israeli banks or the seven Japanese banks, and now with this Bill there will be another seven or eight Arab banks and a number of other banks coming in. When we look at the smaller banks such as the Mercantile, the Canadian Commercial or the Northland, we can see that these banks are going to be up against some very special competition, and the Royal Bank of Canada and the Bank of Montreal are not even going to notice these new banks in place.
What we are going to see as a result of this move is a widespread closing of branch offices across this country, branch offices which exist in small communities and in the rural areas of Canada. These are the banks which are available to the small business people and to the general public. We are suggesting in this Bill that we now bring more of the foreign banks into Canada. The existing cross-subsidization which exists with the larger banks, which enable them to keep open a number of money-losing branches, simply will not be there any longer, Mr. Speaker.
I cannot, for the life of me, see how this Bill is going to benefit Canadians by allowing more foreign involvement in our particular economy. I suspect it is certainly going to result in a greater outflow of banking profits from this country. There have already been concerns raised because of the expanding role of Canadian banks overseas, that certain funds will be moved out of Canada to take advantage of those overseas
Bank Act
opportunities. What I feel is worse than that, Mr. Speaker, is that the profits from these 58 foreign banks, of course, are naturally going to be going back home, to the United States, to Japan or into the European banking system.
The foreign banks would also be less likely to assist in the pursuit of national goals such as the promotion of Canadian exports. Indeed, country lending limits imposed by the parent bank, whether that country be the U.K. or West Germany, could actually hinder the banking subsidiary operating in Canada from financing the sale of Canadian goods to one of the many financially hard-pressed developing countries.
What we are suggesting, then, is that at a time when we should be asking our banks to work with us in pursuing certain goals as a nation, goals which would see the economy revived and some direction in terms of economic development and investment, we are asking our friendly foreigners to join with us in this endeavour. We are asking them to act against their own set of priorities.
I am very concerned about this particular Bill and I am concerned that it is being brought forward in this particular fashion. I am concerned that it is not going to assist us in terms of providing greater competition, although the challenge will now be there. I believe that, as we work toward the next major change to the Bank Act, because of the fact that this concession has been given to the foreign banks by the Government, the foreign banks in the months and years ahead will have to indicate to the Government very clearly that a major portion of their loan portfolio has been moved into the small business sector and that a major part of their banking business has been done in co-operation with credit unions or other financial institutions. We are really tossing the ball now, Mr. Speaker, into the court of the foreign banks and saying to them, "Now that we have allowed you to increase your roll from an 8 per cent to a 16 per cent ceiling, we want to see some benefit accruing to the average Canadian citizen and to the small business community."
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that we are very concerned about the nature of this particular Bill. We stand unconvinced that it is in the best interests of our country or that Canadians are going to benefit. As a matter of fact, from some of the points which have been made, Mr. Speaker, we are convinced that the net result will be a loss to Canadians, that in fact the existing level of the banking and financial services will deteriorate as a result of the so-called competition which these additional 58 banks-and likely to be more-will offer the people of Canada. So we will be opposing this particular Bill with some enthusiasm.

Mr. Speaker, contrary to the previous speaker, I must say that I support this Bill wholeheartedly. I believe the more competition which we can get in our banking service and banking facilities, the better off we are going to be. We are a trading nation. Exports are more important to us than probably to any other nation of our size. I believe the Schedule "B" banks, with additional capital, will help us with some of that export financing.

June 28, 1984
Bank Act
The subject matter of Bill C-30 was before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs several weeks ago and, after hearing from witnesses that included the Inspector General of Banks, representatives from the Schedule "B" banks and representatives from the Trust Companies Association, the committee unanimously recommended that Schedule "B" banks be allowed to increase their capital base in their operations in Canada. As you are aware, the present Act limits the assets of Schedule "B" banks to 8 per cent of the total domestic assets of Canadian banks, as shown on a schedule prepared at the time that provision was enacted. The committee recommended that the 8 per cent limit specified in the legislation be lifted. This recommendation was based on the advice of the Inspector General of Banks that adequate control could be exercised by monitoring the deemed authorized capital of the Schedule "B" banks. However, when the Bill came through, it did not follow the recommendation but it raised the limit from 8 per cent to 16 per cent of the total domestic assets of all banks in Canada. That is the matter we are dealing with today.
We, of course, support Bill C-30 notwithstanding representations made to the committee. I understand the Canadian Bankers' Association supports the Bill, but some members of the CBA are not happy with it and would like to see this Act used as a lever against certain governments which will not grant reciprocal arrangements to our banks. There is another matter of the extra-territorial application of the law of a country against a Canadian bank where its court levied substantial fines for non-compliance. I understand that both these matters are the subject of discussion at a ministerial level and a resolution may be forthcoming. The request of the trust companies association was more direct. In effect they asked that we not pass this Bill until we have dealt with the trust companies, insurance companies and other financial institutions.
The Minister of State for Finance (Mr. MacLaren) has set in motion a committee of representatives from trust companies, insurance companies and other financial institutions to get their recommendations as to where they should fit in a new expanded picture of financial services. Certainly they want to broaden their base of operations to utilize their substantial cash flows. Some would alter their base so as not to be so dependent on one service. I agree that we should await the report and have discussion with the provinces so as to prevent the sort of jungle that was developing in the trust industry through unclear jurisdiction between federally and provincially chartered trust companies. Certainly there is a need to overhaul the legislation covering trust companies, insurance companies and other financial institutions. But while we want to see this matter dealt with on an urgent basis, we did not feel we should hold back this matter until we could deal with that larger question.
We are constantly being told that we must find a solution to higher interest rates. Perhaps competition is the best solution. We noted, when the trust companies ran mortgage rates up to
21 per cent and locked in the mortgages with unreasonable penalties for prepayment, that our chartered banks found themselves very liquid because of a low level of demand of commercial loans. They moved into the mortgage field, and the rates came tumbling down. The trust companies followed the bank led mortgage rates down the scale until housing starts increased and the sluggish real estate market came alive.
Perhaps what we are doing here today will have a ripple effect and with more money available in the market-place the rates may modify. Of course, the one action that may defeat this is if the Government of Canada moves to take a larger piece of the money market. In the past year it took about 75 per cent of the money available in the commercial market, thus making it difficult for those businesses which need term money to find adequate sources. It is plain for anyone to see that we need a more active equity market. Most of our businesses have equity problems. Many have serious cash flow difficulties as they adjust to the regime of low inventories on hand and "just-in-time" suppliers. We wish to co-operate and pass this Bill through all stages so that we may send it to the Senate which we hope will deal with it on a priority basis.

Mr. Speaker, it is my intention to speak fairly briefly on this matter in support of Bill C-30 to amend the Bank Act. I am certainly in general agreement with the idea that foreign banks be allowed to operate in Canada. Since we started this experiment some years ago with an initial 8 per cent ceiling, the experience has been good on balance. It has added competition in the banking field, of which I would like to give you a couple of illustrations.
The first that comes to mind is in the market for municipal loans. I know one or two municipalities in my area which wanted to borrow money but were not able to do so at competitive rates from the Canadian chartered banks. However, they were able to do so from foreign banks which were looking for customers and very interested in this particular market. Another example, on a geographic basis this time, is the market for loans to people in the oil and gas field, not necessarily the big operators, the Essos and the Domes- although some of the people who lent money to Dome will have wished they had not-however, the people in the shipping and other businesses ancillary to oil and gas exploration and production. When the National Energy Program killed the oil and gas business generally in western Canada, the banks, the headquarters or the regional offices of which were in Calgary, automatically came up with the idea that they were not to make loans to people who were dependent on the oil and gas industry because that industry was pretty sick as the result of Liberal Government policy. However, in the Beaufort Sea the opposite was happening. There the exploration business was booming, so to speak. But the operators there found themselves caught up in the same net because the banks with which they dealt had their offices in Calgary where things were going badly. A number of people and businesses in that area were unable to borrow money from the Canadian banks at reasonable rates, if at all, but they were able to borrow money from the foreign banks.
June 28, 1984

These are two illustrations of how the presence of foreign banks in the Canadian lending market can be an advantage to Canadian municipal taxpayers on the one hand and small and medium-sized businessmen on the other. I do not know where the 8 per cent limit came from. It was probably a compromise between 5 per cent and 10 per cent. I do not know where the 16 per cent comes from in this Bill but it seems to me to be a reasonable figure. I do not know why it is 16 per cent rather than 15 per cent or 17 per cent or 18 per cent. Perhaps that can be explained to us. But it would seem to be a reasonable figure. Recommendations have been made that there be no restrictions on them, that foreign banks be allowed to do as much business as they can get without any restrictions. I think it is prudent of us at the present time to continue with the experiment, so to speak, and raise that ceiling. However, we should have some ceiling there for the time being. Perhaps in a few years we could review the situation again and elevate the ceiling or remove it in its entirety.
Others have argued that there should be no restrictions. I have some doubts about that. Although the amount of lending which can be done and the amount of assets which a foreign bank can hold are controlled, I do not think we have quite as much control over a foreign subsidiary as we do over a Canadian bank. I am going to argue this in reverse order. A few years ago in the halcyon days the banks were making a lot of money and lending money to Third World nations. That was the business to be in. That was where the big profits were in banking. I remember the Canadian banks coming to the standing committee and arguing that the reserve requirements imposed upon them should be removed or reduced in respect of loans which Canadian banks were making overseas. When you start reducing the reserves which a bank is required to hold in respect of loans it has made, you are getting on shaky ground. Everyone knows that any system of fractional reserve banking is inherently insolvent. It is incumbent upon governments to prescribe certain mandatory reserves in respect of loans which have been made.
I suspect that the arguments which were made by Canadian banks at that time may well have come back to haunt them, because a lot of the loans that were made offshore prove to be of doubtful value today. The same argument which was used at that time by Canadian banks in their efforts to enhance their profitability overseas has probably been made by foreign banks in their country of origin. In certain circumstances there is a likelihood that foreign banks may be more shaky than our Canadian banks. To a certain extent we must protect the interest of Canadians who make deposits in these banks.
In view of the time and the amount of further business which the House has to do this evening, I think those are the main points which I would like to make. Although there are one or two small additional ones that I would like to make. I listened with interest to the remarks made by the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis). He was presenting the official NDP position. However, I hope that he was really trying to encourage the foreign banks to be more
Bank Act
competitive and to stay honest. I hope that was the intent of what he was saying.
In conclusion, I would like to register some concern about a matter which has already been alluded to by the Hon. Member for York North (Mr. Gamble) with regard to banks from countries which do not allow Canadian banks to operate in their countries. There ought to be reciprocity. If we allow banks from another country to operate in Canada, they ought to allow our banks to operate in their country. One of the biggest bugbears here is France. France will not allow our banks to operate in their country, but presumably we allow French banks to operate in Canada. I would encourage the Government, through the Department of External Affairs, to try to get agreements with countries whose banks we allow to operate in Canada so that they will allow our banks to operate in their country.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Are there any questions or comments? The Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) on debate.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to say a few words on this Bill which is to accommodate foreign banks. In this session we passed the Bank Act which allows foreign banks to work in Canada to the extent of 8 per cent of the Canadian market. A couple of years later a number of banks are close to reaching this level and we are suddenly going to accommodate them.
I have heard Members on both sides of the House talk about how much they abhor the control of the economy which foreign corporations have. If they could possibly get rid of it they would like to do so. Foreign business and financial institutions have such a hold on the country that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) admits daily that we are unable to do anything about the interest rates. Does the Government think that by adding foreign banks and increasing their control of the country we are going to improve that situation? At the moment, every time profits are made by a corporation in Canada they are either sent out of the country or used to buy up more of the country. Does the Government think that by increasing the amount of investment by foreign banks in the country and allowing them to get a greater control of the financial structure we will improve the situation?
Instead of giving foreign banks extra control over the economy, we should be giving the Government the structure to allow it to take much more control of the economy than the Minister of Finance suggests it is able to take at present. These foreign banks have suddenly decided that Canada is a very lucrative market which they can enter with very little investment. They can move their money in here and maintain one office to supply other banks or only large business corporations. As my colleague pointed out, we know that 70 per cent of the assets of foreign banks in Canada has been lent to corporations with yearly revenues in excess of $80 million. They are obviously going for the lucrative and large markets. That is not going to help the man on the street.

June 28, 1984
Bank Act
Canadian banks are in support of accepting foreign banks into the market. They have told us that they want this. They support this move because the "big five" are not really worried about this little bit of competition. It will give them a lever for investing in other countries. I suggest that we should perhaps study this. Is the ability of our so-called Canadian banks to invest in foreign countries going to help our economy? Is it going to put the man on the street to work? Will it help the unemployment situation at all? We are ignoring the basic requirements that would help the economy of this country and would make a difference to the man on the street. Instead, the Government and the Opposition are accommodating the large banks in Canada and the foreign banks, which really cannot be expected to make decisions that are in the best interest of Canadians. Consequently, we are opposed to this Bill and would rather not see it come forward. It does give an indication of the priority which the Official Opposition and the Government gives to the financial institutions of Canada which are in the process of selling us out to foreign countries as much as possible and will continue to do so.
Canadians must consider a government which will move away from large financial institutions. Perhaps that will be the issue in the next election; large corporations against the people. The Official Opposition and the Government will be led by leaders whose real responsibility is not to the people of Canada but to the large corporations in Canada that are closely connected to the foreign banks. It has been shown here this evening that both of those Parties support the take-over of Canada by foreign interests.

speechtext: that Bill C-24, an Act to amend the Financial Administration Act in relation to Crown corporations and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates, be concurred in.

He said: Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to take part in the debate on third reading of Bill C-24 and to speak briefly about a Bill which has been changed through amendments that were worked out through the efforts of members of all Parties. Because of this agreement, it is clear that this Bill will be adopted by the time the House adjourns tomorrow.
The Bill, as amended, speaks highly indeed of what can be the effectiveness of our parliamentary process, especially committee stage, and of a willingness on the part of the Government, the Official Opposition and other Hon. Members to consider carefully and respond to the views expressed about the Bill, including those of witnesses at the committee and key people such as the Auditor General, those in the business community, the arts community and other interested groups like the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants.
Mr. Speaker, the Government and the Opposition have worked together to make a practical and effective Bill, a Bill of which all Members may be proud. Our joint efforts in the course of this parliamentary process will result in the first major and successful update in more than thirty years of the legal framework that provides for control and accountability with respect to Crown corporations. That is no small achievement.
The purpose of Bill C-24 is to clarify the roles and responsibilities of the corporations' chief executive officers and boards of directors, of Ministers, the Government and Parliament, and to establish this updated legal framework for control and accountability of Crown corporations. Mr. Speaker, the Bill, including the amendments on which agreement was reached in committee, will provide that framework. I would now like to highlight very briefly the main amendments that were made.

There has been much discussion about the inclusion of the cultural corporations in the legislation in its original form. One of the major concerns expressed has been that from the point of view of the arts community, the legislation appeared to give too much authority over program priorities of the cultural corporations. Therefore, in response to these concerns, the Canada Council, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the National Arts Centre and the Canadian Film Development Corporation will not be covered by this Bill. It is the Government's intention to clarify its accountability framework for them and other cultural corporations, where necessary, through separate legislative measures.
In drafting this Bill, we intended that it would be binding on the Crown, and we obtained the view of the Department of

June 28, 1984
Financial Administration Act
Justice that this was the case. However, the Bill as amended will eliminate any uncertainty in this regard.
In view of the concern expressed about the special motion procedure for creating parent Crown corporations set forth in the original version of this Bill, the Bill as amended will provide that all parent Crown corporations would be created through Acts of Parliament, subject, of course, to the rules of the House. In this connection, it has been agreed that the Bill as amended would remove those provisions in certain pieces of existing legislation which allow a Minister to create Crown corporations, with the exception of the Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act and the Canada Ports Corporation Act, two Acts only recently adopted by Parliament. This change responds to a concern of the Auditor General.
It has always been the Government's contention through this Bill to have a strengthened role for the boards of directors of our Crown corporations and to set out clearly how they and the senior officers would be appointed and held accountable for the corporations' conduct of their affairs. In order to clarify this intention, the Bill as amended would provide that the Board of Directors would be appointed by the appropriate Minister with the approval of the Governor in Council. The chairman and the chief executive officer would be appointed by the Governor in Council, but only after the board of directors has been consulted by the appropriate Minister. Additionally, the Canada Post Corporation Act would be amended so that vice-presidents of that organization as well would be appointed by its board of directors.
The Bill as amended will provide that henceforth for all new parent Crown corporations, all officer appointments other than chairman and chief executive officers would be made by the board of directors. As well, the appropriate Minister, representing the sole shareholder, would be responsible for the appointment and removal of all non-officer directors, subject to the approval of the Governor in Council. Furthermore, wording has been added to the Bill to specify sanctions for wilful neglect of duties by corporation officers.
Concerns were expressed about the role given to Ministers in the version of the Bill originally presented to this House. To respond to these concerns, a statement has been inserted in the Bill, the one that appears in the current Financial Administration Act that, "each crown corporation is ultimately accountable through the appropriate Minister to Parliament for the conduct of the affairs of the corporation." This amendment responds to another concern raised by the Auditor General.
Still another concern of the Auditor General was with respect to the criteria for the scheduling of the various Crown corporations. As a result, the Bill has been amended to provide that Crown corporations would be scheduled in Part II of Schedule C only if, in the opinion of the Governor in Council, they operate in a manner generally independent of operating appropriations and in a competitive commercial environment. A section will be added which will state that no corporation can be added to Part I or Part II unless, in the opinion of the Governor in Council, that corporation would not more appropriately be placed in Schedule B.
The Bill has been amended to respond to concerns expressed by the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants. First, we have deleted from the Bill all provisions that would allow Treasury Board to authorize departures from the generally accepted accounting principles in the preparation of the financial statements of Crown corporations. Second, the auditor of a Crown corporation now would be granted qualified privilege similar to that provided by Section 166 of the Canada Business Corporations Act so that he or she would be protected from liability in respect of statements made fairly in the discharge of his or her duties. The auditor's report would be addressed to the appropriate Minister and it would include separate opinions on both financial and non-financial information.
In addition to the changes in the Bill that I have just highlighted, it has been changed by a number of other amendments of a technical nature which obviously the House would not expect me to describe in detail at this point in time.
To conclude, I would like to extend my thanks to all Members in the House who have participated in the debate on this Bill and in the development of amendments to turn it into what I believe Members of the House will agree is a very good piece of legislation. I would like to particularly extend my thanks to the Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson), chief spokesperson on Crown corporation policy for the Official Opposition. He has spoken out consistently and forcefully for an effective and workable Bill.
I want to recognize again the efforts of the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), my Parliamentary Secretary. The agreement on the amendments to the Bill and the working out of an agreement for a short time frame for its passage is to a large part a result of the efforts of these two Members. It shows the kind of co-operative activity that can be found in this House when it is operating at its best.
I want to again recognize the co-operative spirit in which the Official Opposition and other Members of this House have approached the matters of amendments and of the allocation of time to enable the Bill to pass before the House adjourns tomorrow. This Bill will put in place for the benefit of all Canadians an effective new framework for the control and accountability of these important corporate instruments of public policy. I commend this Bill to this House for its support in the interest of good administration of our Crown corporations and the over-all public interest.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Minister for his kind remarks. I rise to speak this evening on Bill C-24 as amended with mixed emotions. This will almost certainly be my last speech in the House of Commons before returning to private life. I must admit to a sense of satisfaction tinged with irony that my last speech will relate to this Crown corporations Bill.
I have spent a great deal of time and energy over the past year studying the subject of Crown corporations in my capacity of co-chairman of our Party task force on Crown corporations. I shared the chairmanship of that task force with
June 28, 1984

Senator Bill Kelly and we spent the last nine months studying most of the aspects of Crown corporations and how our new Government should address the problem.
Indeed, it is a major problem with which we must deal. After all, we are today talking about over 300 Crown corporations with assets in the neighbourhood of $70 billion and liabilities in the neighbourhood of $80 billion. They cost the taxpayers somewhere between $5 billion and $10 billion a year. It is a major problem, one with which this Government and our previous Government lived for the last ten years. I suppose we have lived with the problem for longer than that, but the problem has grown and certainly the number of dollars involved has increased over the last ten years.
Some of my colleagues know that I have often been frustrated and disenchanted with the role of back-bench Member of Parliament, frustrated and disenchanted with the lack of impact a Member can have on the issues that come before this House, whether they be great or small. I have learned to appreciate the wisdom of a gentleman by the name of Walter Bagehot who wrote in 1867 that a Member of Parliament must sacrifice not only his time, his labour and his money to be a Member of Parliament, but perhaps the greatest sacrifice of all is the sacrifice of his mind. I am therefore pleased to note that my colleagues and I on this side of the House at least played a major role in the improvement of Bill C-24 from the state it was in when it was initially introduced. After long and arduous discussions and negotiations, we on this side of the House proposed roughly 100 amendments, many of which were accepted by the Government and now form a part of the Bill that is before us.
One of the major amendments we were able to have accepted was the removal of clauses that would have allowed the Government to continue to set up new Crown corporations with little or no control by Parliament. We were able to enhance and clarify the role of the individual Minister. We took a significant step forward in creating ministerial accountability. After all, ministerial accountability is one of the key factors in coming to grips with the accountability of Crown corporations. We were also able to increase the amount and quality of information provided to Parliament.
Another important amendment attained by the Conservative Party was the protection for the unique and historic independence of our cultural organizations. The Canada Council, the NAC, the CBC and the Canadian Film Development Corporation will no longer fall under the jurisdiction of the legislation amended by Bill C-24. Since 1979, the Progressive Conservative Party has supported the concept of a separate cultural agencies Act, an Act which would set cultural agencies entirely apart from other Crown corporations. In his statement agreeing to exempt the cultural corporations, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) has committed the Government to that concept.
I am gratified that we were able to have that impact on the Bill, and the impact of the many other amendments which were reflected in the legislation. I only regret that we did not have time to do more, and that we were not allowed to have
Financial Administration Act
the same impact on the majority of Bills that came before this House, including many of the Bills with which I have been associated since I have been a Member of this House of Commons. It is reassuring to know that every once in awhile, the House of Commons does in fact work.
Do not misunderstand me. This is an imperfect Bill. I suppose one could say that to find a perfect Bill in an imperfect world is beyond human capacity. Nevertheless, this is an imperfect Bill. It goes only part way toward addressing the serious problems that have bedevilled Crown corporations. The process by which the Bill was prepared certainly left a lot to be desired.
As we look back over the last decade, we see a host of scandals in which Crown corporations were involved. We have seen studies done ad nauseam about what to do with Crown corporations. There have been royal commissions, commissions of inquiry, white papers, blue papers and previous Bills all the way back to 1972. Yet I must condemn the Government for waiting for over ten years until the dying days of this Parliament, and very likely the dying days of this Government, to table this complex and very difficult Bill. After waiting for ten years, the Government asks for passage of the Bill in only two months.
In my short time in public life and, as a matter of fact, in my private life as well, I must say that I have never seen anything in such a state of shambles as this Bill was when it came before the committee after second reading. The final package of amendments reviewed by the committee was almost two inches thick. Right up until the last moment, the Government was bringing in housekeeping, technical and other amendments. The last minute changes were so extensive that I understood it would take three days to print the Bill. It is a miracle that it could be printed in three days.
In its haste to move the Bill forward, the Government apparently tried to intimidate Crown corporations into not airing publicly their problems with the Bill and not appearing before the Parliamentary Committee.
Francis Fox gave the orders too.

As I said, this is an imperfect Bill. It is a far cry from what we on this side think is necessary.
I am afraid to say that Bill C-24 will, I believe, cause a further bureaucratization of Crown corporations, something which I do not think is in the best interests of our attempt to bring Crown corporations under control. The Bill does not go far enough in so far as describing the role of the board of directors. I happen to believe that the board of directors has a very, very vital role to play in the control and management of Crown corporations. If they are not given anything to do, if they are not part of the chain of accountability, from the chief executive officer to the board of directors to the Minister, and if they are not allowed to function in a manner in which they can financially control that corporation, they will not be able to respect their position of responsibility.

June 28, 1984
Financial Administration Act
However, improvements have been made. While many of those changes are worthwhile, the Bill still confuses and obscures ministerial responsibility for Crown corporations. It confuses what the Lambert Commission referred to as the vital chain of accountability to Parliament. I am afraid that this legislation ignores many of the issues which we think Crown corporation legislation should address.
One of the most vital issues which is not addressed in the legislation-and I hope that a future Progressive Conservative government will come to grips with it-is the appointment of a chief executive officer. As long as the chief executive officer's appointment process is retained as a Prime Ministerial prerogative, instead of being an appointment which is made by the board of directors, the chief executive officer will never be accountable to the board of directors and the board of directors will never be able to hold that chief executive officer accountable. When that chain of accountability is broken, we cannot expect to receive the measure of control which I believe is necessary to protect Canadian taxpayers.
As well, the complex and contentious subject of privileges and immunities which are enjoyed by Crown corporations has not been dealt with.
Another very serious problem which I feel most strongly about is the creation of a standing committee of this House-I would prefer it to be a joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons-to deal specifically with the subject of Crown corporations. As I said earlier when introducing my remarks, the area of Crown corporations is a huge one within the federal Government's domain. The standing committees of this House simply do not have the time to deal with the review of mandates of Crown corporations on a continuing basis. Crown corporations must have a review of their annual reports, operating plans, capital budgets and corporate plans. It is an immense undertaking for Parliament to monitor Crown corporations. There simply is not enough time for the existing standing committees to do that. If this Parliament is going to offer a measure of control on behalf of Canadian taxpayers, I feel very strongly that a standing committee of the House should be created.
With all the deficiencies in the Bill which I have indicated, why have we decided to let the Bill go through? The decision was certainly not easy. Many of my colleagues are still less than enthusiastic about the passage of this legislation in its present form. In so far as I am concerned, I had a good many anguished moments in committee and have had anguished moments since that time. We will pass this Bill because we realize that it is impractical to expect anything better at this time from this Government. It is impractical to think that it could prepare alternative legislation within the time it has left.
Second, much of what is good about this Bill stems from many of the initiatives which my colleagues and myself have taken on this side of the House. We were reluctant to see all of our efforts go for nothing.
Third, we did not want to send to Crown corporations another message after all these years that the passage of any Crown corporation legislation by Parliament was not possible. We did not want to confirm the impression that Crown corporations can sit in isolation, immune from review by Parliament. Further, we did not want to send a message to future governments, whether they be Liberal or Conservative, that the passage of even a half-hearted Crown corporation Bill was politically impossible.
Finally, having rescued the cultural organizations from Bill C-24, we wanted to entrench their separate status before the Government had a chance to change its mind. Therefore, reluctantly and with many misgivings, we have decided to let Bill C-24 pass.
Most of the real problems which Crown corporations face will have to wait for the advent of a new government which will be free from the legacy of the past, willing to take a hard look at the problems and possible solutions, and with the political will to be a vigilant and intelligent shareholder. All the legislation in the world can be written about Crown corporations, but we will never be able to come to grips with the problems without political will. It requires the political will of the Prime Minister, and the Cabinet to control and manifest a regime of proper accountability. I look forward to that day. I only regret that we missed that golden opportunity in Bill C-24. I also regret that I will not be here to see it happen. In the meantime, Bill C-24, such as it is, will have to do.
I would like to extend my thanks to the clerk and the people who worked so hard in committee. I think that thanks should go as well to some of the bureaucrats for their efforts and the time which they spent in the preparation of this Bill. Those who think that all of our bureaucrats are "nine to fivers" are operating under a great misapprehension.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, my intervention on this Bill will be very brief, because I think the Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson) said it all. I would like to begin by complimenting the Hon. Member for Calgary South and the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) who have by the process of negotiation come forth with a Bill which at least serves notice on Crown corporations that Parliament feels some responsibility for them and that in the future they will have to understand that their position is relative to Parliament's need for them. I feel we have gone on long enough with Crown corporations which have been given a mandate, have been organized and then have quickly forgotten their mandate and gone their own way to become organizations with their own ends in mind and with very little accountability to the Parliament of Canada.
I have really two points to make. First, the process which took place in this particular Bill needs to be looked at very closely by this Parliament. It is a process which we should try and emulate in many other Bills. We had put before us a bill
June 28, 1984

which had been created by the bureaucrats, by the Minister, the Deputy Minister and had gone down through the system. It had behind it the prestige of the department and the people who had created it. Only the circumstance of this particular situation allowed us to take a look at this Bill in a way which made it possible for the opposition to have some kind of an input. If there had not been the leadership race, if there had not been the time limitation on the Government to get the Bill through, it may not have been the case that the ideas of the Opposition were accommodated.
I strongly believe that the process which was forced on the Government because of this Bill is the kind of process which would make the best use of parliamentarians, because it allowed this Parliament to recognize the quality and ability of all Hon. Members of Parliament to make a contribution to legislation instead of just government Members and the bureaucrats behind that Government. I believe it is very important that this kind of procedure be incorporated into the traditions of Parliament at some time in the future for the good of Canada.
Another point I want to make is that for years this Government and other Governments have tried to establish some kind of accountability for Crown corporations and have, to a great extent, failed. This Bill may have warts. I am not going to go through the shortcomings which we suggest are in this Bill. However, as I mentioned before, it will serve notice on Crown corporations that Hon. Members on all sides of this House are not going to let them go their own way in the future. By passing this Bill we are saying that from now on we want to be sure that the mandate which is given to a Crown corporation is adhered to. We want to be sure that the expenditures of money by Crown corporations are made at the behest of Parliament, not at the behest of a member of Cabinet or the Cabinet itself. This Bill does not do this entirely, but we are serving notice that this is the direction in which we want to go. I feel it is a very important Bill in that way. It does not go far enough, Mr. Speaker, but it does go in the right direction.
I have to agree entirely with the Hon. Member for Calgary South, that even if we put an absolutely perfect Bill in place- which this Bill is not-we would still require the political will of the Government of the day to have the kind of accountability from Crown corporations which this Parliament has indicated it wants. After almost five years on the Public Accounts Committee, I know that Hon. Members of this House, regardless from which Party they come, do want accountability of Crown corporations. The process we went through in getting at least a portion of that accountability is a valuable experience for this House which we would extend possibly to other Bills. I hope whichever Government is in power after the next election it will take a look at this Bill and see that there are still some things which are not the way they should be and change them, so that eventually those Crown corporations which are already in place, as well as future Crown corporations, will be instruments of public policy and will be controlled by the Parliament of Canada for the people of Canada.
Financial Administration Act
Crown corporations have a role to play in the economy of Canada, but that role is only worthwhile if they are instruments of the Government and controlled by this Parliament. Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker, and I say to you that we will be supporting this Bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice Foster (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my purpose to speak at length tonight. I believe there was an understanding that we would have about 20 minutes on each side with only two speakers for the Official Opposition and the Government. I believe my Minister has taken up almost all of the time which would have been available to me.
I just want to say how pleased I am to see this Bill finally come out of committee and get to third reading tonight. I believe it is an important piece of legislation which will have far-reaching implications for the Crown corporations which daily affect the lives of Canadians. We only have to think about Petro-Canada, Air Canada, CNR or any of the other commercially competitive Crown corporations, as well as the many other corporations which serve the needs of Canadians on behalf of the Government of Canada, to realize that this Bill has very far-reaching effects.
I want to pay tribute, as did the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray), to the kind of co-operation which existed between Hon. Members of the Opposition and the New Democratic Party, especially the Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson), the Hon. Member for Rosedale (Mr. Crom-bie), the Hon. Member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty), and the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hov-debo), because without that kind of co-operation in moving and dealing with amendments at committee stage, and agreeing to work long hours all of this week, we obviously could never have moved this Bill out of committee late this morning and into the House tonight. I believe we had over 100 speakers on second reading in the seven days of debate. Therefore, since March 16, when this Bill was introduced, it has been a long and tortuous period of time.
I also want to pay tribute to the Clerk of the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee who worked all through last night on the amendments to the Bill. I also understand that some 12 or 15 people on the task force from the Treasury Board have been working for over eight or nine months on this Bill, many of whom are in the gallery tonight. As well, the Department of Justice officials worked through the night last night on the amendments.
I believe this Bill, with the amendments we have added, really meets many of the ideas which the Government had in mind in its original introduction. There have been a lot of compromises and the President of the Treasury Board and the Government have accepted many amendments. I think in all cases we are agreed that we have strengthened the Bill and the role of Parliament, both in the creation of Crown corporations and in the supervision of budgets and so on. I just want to express my appreciation to all those who have made the passage of this Bill possible. I think it will really meet the

June 28, 1984
Financial Administration Act
needs of Canadians regarding these important institutions of the federal Government.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to say that I came here tonight not to bury the Bill but to praise it. That is a tremendous change from the second reading debate which was marked by a good deal of very deep and divergent feelings on both sides of the House. Frankly, I did not expect that I would have the opportunity to say that I believe we have a Bill which is vastly improved and which will improve considerably on the status quo for Canadians.
Going back to 1979 and the days of the Clark Government,
1 had the responsibility for drafting legislation which would serve as an omnibus Bill to bring control and accountability to Crown corporations. What was so striking to me at that time and remains so today is the tremendous range, power and cost of Crown corporations which extend into virtually every aspect of Canadian life. It was made apparent to me that these Crown corporations, many of which had served useful purposes at the time they were set up, and continue to do so, had in many instances moved well beyond the purposes intended by Parliament. In some instances Parliament and perhaps even the Government were not aware of even the existence of some Crown corporations. Certainly it became apparent that parliamentary and governmental controls were weak or non-existent in many instances. It was essential that legislation be put in place that would vastly improve the quality of the relationship between Crown corporations and the government and people of Canada.
I want to make reference to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson). As he said, what we heard tonight was his last speech as a Member of the House of Commons, unless through some measure which would be of great surprise to all of us we found ourselves back here in the fall. I had the pleasure of working with the Hon. Member and I can tell you that he is a tremendously diligent and hard working, conscientious and principled person. The House will be poorer for the fact he has decided not to stand for re-election. He has another quality, one of modesty. One of the things he did not do was to take credit for the fairly dramatic improvements which have taken place in this Bill as a direct result of his efforts and those of Members on this side under his leadership.
When the Hon. Member for Calgary South co-chaired the PC task force on Crown corporations with Senator Bill Kelly, they launched an energetic schedule which was designed to develop a set of principles which would be useful for a PC Government or the present government in trying to come to grips with the control and accountability of Crown corporations. As one who has seen the results of that task force, I can tell you that is one of the finest pieces of work ever to have been done by a group of parliamentarians, certainly in the 12 years in which I have been in Ottawa. The report speaks volumes about the conscientiousness of the Hon. Member.
However, what speaks equally well of his work are the dramatic improvements made in this Bill as a direct result of his leadership. The Hon. Member is a very modest man, but I think I can say this is a good day for Parliament because of the Hon. Member's leadership. We have been able to remove provisions from this Bill which would have allowed the Government to do an end run around Parliament. If the Bill as originally drafted had passed, we would likely never again have seen the Government come to Parliament with a special act to incorporate a new Crown corporation. There were easier measures which would have allowed them to put it through Parliament with virtually no study or debate. It is a victory for the taxpayers of Canada because we have had better controls placed on Crown corporations to ensure that their financial management is conducted in a more business-like, sane and rational manner. The changes improved upon both the original draft and upon the status quo. That, again, is a victory for the Hon. Member for Calgary South and for my colleagues.
It is a victory as well for the Progressive Conservative Party. Under the leadership of our colleague from Calgary South, we fought hard to have amendments made which would make this bill infinitely better than what it would have been if the Government had been able to force it through in its original state. I think the Hon. Member, as he prepares to leave the House of Commons, can take considerable satisfaction in his work.
Hear, hear!

He leaves us as well with a commitment. The position in which my Party finds itself tonight is that we have a Bill infinitely preferable to what it would have been if we had not fought this fight. No question about that. If the Government had all the time in the world and all the numbers to get its way, then the Bill would not have been what it is today. He has given us a much better Bill. He has also put us in a position where we have gone part of the way towards achieving the goals he set out as chairman of the PC task force on Crown corporations. There is more work to be done, as he pointed out. In many ways, the Bill is deficient. One of the things he did not mention would be the controls on subsidiary corporations. We should have had a better definition as well of the implications of agent of Her Majesty status and the immunities and privileges that Crown corporations claim on the marketplace.
Notwithstanding the fact the Bill is flawed, we have moved well along the way and we now have a vehicle in place where, if there is a PC Government following the next election, we can make the amendments to bring the Bill to the stage where it is consistent with what we have recommended to the Canadian people and Parliament. That will be a considerably less time consuming process for this Parliament and the people of Canada than it would have been had we had to reinvent the wheel. That in itself is to the credit of the Hon. Member and he can take considerable satisfaction from that. He will be able to see his efforts continuing long after he has left this place.
June 28, 1984

I am pleased by another amendment made to this Bill. Wearing my hat briefly as the joint chairman of the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments, I know that my co-chairman, Senator John Godfrey, would also be pleased to see that the rights and position of that committee have been respected as a result of the amendments made to this Bill. That is positive. I am pleased as well that the traditional arm's length relationship between the Government and the cultural corporations, which is so essential if they are to preserve their integrity and if there is to be any confidence in the ability of the Canada Council to function free of government manipulation and interference, has been maintained. That is a significant victory. In addition, one of the great concerns Members on this side have had has been with the creation of the Canada Development Investment Corporation. If the new leader of the Liberal Party decides to dissolve the House after the swearing in on Saturday, we will have achieved a major victory in that the CDIC will not have be forced through Parliament. A new government will have to be seized with the issue of what to do with this massive holding company which has tremendous scope to interfere in virtually all aspects of commerce in Canada. From the vantage point of Members on this side of the House, that in itself is a very significant victory again.
This Bill has had provisions included in it that ensure that the passage of this Bill in no way means the Government will not have to worry about coming to Parliament with specific legislation if it hopes to have CDIC recognized and appropriations going directly to the parent corporation.
I do not want to go on at great length, because the Parliamentary Secretary indicated there was a disposition in the House to act quickly. I want to acknowledge the flexibility shown by the President of the Treasury Board, and I might also single out the Parliamentary Secretary himself. His genial good humour, even in times of considerable disagreement was very helpful in keeping lines of communication open and ensuring that this sort of agreement could be reached. I think he deserves credits for doing that.
I would also like to pay tribute to my colleague from Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo). During the time he has served on the Public Accounts committee, and also during his time on this committee, he has demonstrated that he has a genuine desire to see proper controls placed on Crown corporations to ensure that the rights of the taxpayers of Canada and the rights of Parliament are protected and enhanced.
My colleagues have mentioned other people to whom thanks should go. I would like to mention a couple of them. One of them is Mr. Donald Gracey. I first met Mr. Gracey when I was sworn in as Minister of State for the Treasury Board in 1979. I inherited Mr. Gracey who was the Chairman of the Crown corporations task force. At that time he was a senior official in the Privy Council office. It was largely as a result of his efforts that Bill C-27 was drawn up so rapidly and was able to be presented to Parliament within a matter of days of the
Financial Administration Act
Government meeting the House for the first time. Mr. Gracey and many of the members of the Crown corporations task force have moved on to other areas and are not able to see the culmination of their efforts to date. It was those people, with their commitment dating back to over a decade in some cases, who laid the groundwork for any progress which has been made since. Mr. Gracey served both as a consultant to the P.C. Crown corporations task force and also as a consultant to Members on this side of the House as the Bill went before committee. He served us extremely well. We are tremendously grateful to the contributions he has made and tremendously proud to have been able to work with him.
There are others whom I cannot mention tonight. They know who they are. If it had not been for their efforts and their diligence over the years in wanting to see good legislation passed, and fighting against tremendous obstacles to have legislation brought forward which would give some element of control and accountability to ensure that the abuses, scandals and problems which we have seen over the course of the past 15 or 20 years come to an end, there would be no way that we could stand where we do today. Even though they cannot be publicly acknowledged, they have certainly laid a foundation which is essential.
A Progressive Conservative Government will honour their commitment. It will complete the work which has been begun. Their efforts will not be lost or dissipated as a result of having a measure which goes only three-quarters of the way. They deserve to see Parliament passing legislation which does the whole job. Taxpayers, and my colleague from Calgary South deserve to see the whole job being done.
I will not go on at any greater length. I simply want to say that I am pleased to be able to support the Bill at this stage. It is a significant achievement. I want to underscore my thanks to the Member for Calgary South for his leadership. On behalf of my colleagues and I, I would sincerely like to wish him well as he goes on to other pursuits. We have valued his counsel, leadership and friendship.
