Mr. Speaker, if this Bill were given its proper title, it would be called the Regulations Bill. By regulation the Government intends to allegedly correct some of the difficulties faced by people who have approached a lender for the purpose of prepaying a mortgage. If you examine the Bill in detail you will find in Clause 6:
Whenever the amount of principal money expressed to be secured by a mortgage on real property given after the coming into force of this section is greater than such amount as is prescribed by regulation,-
I think it is appropriate to ask why the Government has decided not to disclose exactly what the principle amount should be. It is also appropriate to make that same inquiry with respect to the provisions of Clause 7(1) as they presently appear in the Act. Under Clause 7(1), as amended, we find, among other things that:
-no interest is chargeable, payable or recoverable on the principal money unless the mortgage contains a statement in a form prescribed by regulation showing-
A number of things which are contained in the Act follow. I would have thought that we could have had a schedule attached to this Bill showing the prescribed form. I would also think that the information in Clause 7(1 )(b) might well have been spelled out in the Bill itself. The Section would now read:
-no charge within such classes of charges prescribed by regulation for the purposes of this paragraph is chargeable, payable or recoverable unless the mortgage contains, in the form and manner prescribed by regulation-
We must remember that this Bill was allegedly designed to accomplish a very simple and specific purpose. The purpose was to permit mortgagors to prepay their mortgages, coming up with a figure which they could well understand since the majority of mortgagors are not solicitors but are average individuals in the country who, in large measure, desire to terminate the payments on mortgages secured on their own personal residences. Why is it, therefore, that we have these complicated, convoluted provisions which, I must confess, use every bit of imagination of anyone reading them to understand.
Let us continue on with provisions of the Bill. We find once again that Clause 7(3) on page 3 of the Bill states that paragraph 1(a) does not apply if the information referred to in subparagraphs l(a)(i) and l(a)(ii) was, prior to the execution
of the mortgage, disclosed in a form, once again, prescribed by regulation.
Clause 7(4) provides that paragraph 1(Z?) does not apply with respect to any particular charge within such classes of charges as are prescribed by regulation for the purposes of that paragraph if, prior to the execution of the mortgage, the amount of that charge was disclosed in a form prescribed by regulation.
Then we come to what is surely the most troublesome clause of this Bill. Under what will be amended Clause 11.1 of the Bill, Section 10 and 11 do not apply in such circumstances as are prescribed by regulation.
What this Bill proposes to do is repeal, by regulation, a specific provision of a statute. I submit that that is a process which is not recognized by the law. Parliament enacted Sections 10 and 11 of the Interest Act. Parliament is now providing that those sections may be restricted or eliminated in such circumstances as regulations may require. The proper course for the House is to delete, amend or change sections of existing statutes and not delegate that right to the Governor in Council. That is exactly the process that the Government is undertaking now. It is delegating the right to pass laws and amend existing statutes to the Governor in Council. I submit that that process has no legal foundation. It is improper and beyond the scope of any authority granted to the Governor in Council.
I must say that in the event that we look at the provisions of Section 12.2 as they would be amended, a section which allegedly provides the relief that this Bill is supposed to provide to those people who wish to prepay their mortgages, we find spelled out exactly what the mortgagor must do in order to obtain a discharge. He must pay a number of amounts. The amounts spelled out in the Bill are "(a), the amount of principle money due at the time of the tendering of the payment or such lesser amount of principle money as is allowed by regulation". What are they talking about? When a draftsman prepares such a specific insert in a statute, what does the ordinary home owner calculate as being the principal amount of the mortgage that he must pay when he tenders a payment for the discharge of his mortgage? While he can determine exactly what is the principal amount due under the mortgage, what is this other lesser amount of principal money as is allowed by regulation?
He also must pay the interest on the principal amount. That is the normal, logical and sensible procedure that has taken place since mortgages were invented.
Now comes the crunch. The other amount he must pay is the prepayment charge provided by the regulations, calculated in the manner prescribed by regulation or any other agreed or prepaid charge if it is less than the prepayment charged provided for by the regulations. I do not know what that is and I want to say that neither will the home owner who tenders an amount for payment know what that means.
Obtaining a discharge of a mortgage is a very important facet in the lives of home owners. Let us take the case of
June 28, 1984

someone providing a cheque to a mortgage. The process requires that the cheque must be certified because they will not take an ordinary cheque unless it happens to be with the lending institution on whom the cheque is drawn. If that cheque is $10 too little, that person is still obliged to pay the interest and the mortgagee can refuse to accept payment of that cheque. That individual can go to court and argue that he should have had that discharge because he tendered his payment. If the payment is not in the right amount, interest will run on the principal amount of that outstanding obligation. By the time that individual gets to court and the case is heard two years later, interest will be running on the amount that was not accepted as a proper payment to discharge a mortgage.
Surely some element of certainty must be available for the average citizen who tenders an amount to obtain a discharge of his mortgage. Will this Bill accomplish that purpose? Absolutely not! I do not know what amount that is and neither does the Government House Leader know what that amount would ever be.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What about tabling in the courts?

What we have done as a result of the amendment which will change Section 10 is provide for the elimination of the one thing that the citizen could look to, perhaps with some judicial assistance in connection with what a five-year mortgage is, which is knowing what three months interest by way of bonus discharge meant. That was easy to calculate. The principal amount was spelled out and one could get a computer print-out of the exact calculation. He could calculate the three months' interest bonus and tender that payment, together with the interest due up to the time of tendering. He was entitled to a discharge of his mortgage. He also had to pay a discharge fee which was required. Now he will never know what this amount is because it is a prepayment charge provided for by regulation.
This whole Bill is a fraud. It is pretending to remedy a recognized problem in society but does not do that. The prepayment charge provided for by regulation may be, if the Governor in Council decides, interest at the fixed rate under the mortgage until the end of the term. The House is asked to pass this Bill which leaves in the hands of the Governor in Council the right to determine what that amount is. There is no limitation placed upon the Government. I would be interested to hear the comments of the Government House Leader. It may indeed be the whole amount of interest until the end of the term because we do not know.
Even if the Government was to file the proposed regulations under this Bill with the House today, they could be changed tomorrow. That is the magic of regulations: they do not have to be brought before this place. Parliament will never again see them. The Government alone will decide what the amount is to be. We are asked to pass a Bill which is supposed to provide relief for Canadian home owners. This Bill does not provide that relief. It is an attempt to employ phraseology that is loose and inconclusive. It smokescreens the problems.

Business of the House
With the coming election, I know that Government members will be able to travel throughout the country and say that they have amended the Interest Act so that now there is a method for prepaying a mortgage. It may cost Canadians twice as much as it would have otherwise, but nobody knows. I want to say that this type of legislation which the Government has presented does not do justice to the House and to the duties and obligations imposed upon the members in this place.

Interest Act

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) is rising. Is the Hon. Member rising on the same point of order or is he rising for debate?
Mr. Speaker, I am rising on debate.
The House resumed consideration of the Motion of Mr. Gray, that Bill C-36, an Act to Amend the Interest Act, be now read a third time and do pass.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on Bill C-36. I listened with a considerable amount of interest to the previous speaker. I find myself agreeing with him to a large extent, which surprises me. But nevertheless the arguments he made were more than deserving.
In the last several days I have received a number of phone calls and letters from people asking me when Bill C-36 will pass, giving them a significant amount of interest relief on their mortgages. An impression has been created for some reason or other that Bill C-36 will provide lower interest rates and relief for mortgage holders, or people negotiating a new mortgage from high interest rates or, as we have seen in the last few days, the escalating interest rates. I have had to tell people that that is not the case, that this Act to amend the Interest Act has nothing to do with assisting them with their mortgages. It will not do anything to make life easier for people or enable them to afford a home mortgage during these difficult times. When you think of what it is going to do, I believe the Government has misled the people of Canada.
I recall on many occasions in the House when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) would stand in his place and say that as far as he was concerned a three-month penalty clause on a mortgage being renegotiated to take advantage of a low interest rate as the rates came down was more than appropriate. The Minister felt that that was quite all right, and if we were having any difficulties with lending institutions which were not co-operating that we should send our cases to him and he would take care of these matters. What his term "take care of it" meant was that "I will do nothing except send along your letter to the appropriate financial institution", and whatever the institution decides to do will be appropriate for the Minister of Finance and the Government of Canada. I am afraid that hundreds, perhaps thousands, of Canadians had their hopes lifted in the belief that the Minister of Finance was serious in what he said and that the Government of Canada was prepared to act, only to have those hopes dashed as a result of the phoney and quite inappropriate comments of the Minister.
In essence, what this Bill does is make it clear to people what it will cost them to prepay their loans. I am not certain
how this will assist anybody or how it will make life easier for anybody who has a mortgage at 14 per cent or 15 per cent. Perhaps we might be lucky enough to have interest rates drop to 10 per cent or 11 per cent, and therefore be able to renegotiate a mortgage to take advantage of improved times. But this Bill does nothing for that situation.
This Bill misrepresents to the people of Canada what the Government is doing. The Government is attempting in this pre-election period to give the impression that we are amending the Interest Act to assist people who have home mortgages or who would like to take out a home mortgage. The Bill will do virtually nothing for the hundreds of thousands of Canadians who find themselves pressed up against the wall as a result of today's high interest rates. It will not bring any relief to any of those people. The Bill will not assist anybody in terms of being a home owner. Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, the Bill is a bit of a sham.
I, for one, am looking forward to an election campaign when people in an assembly will say to a Liberal candidate: Surely, the Government has taken action to provide assistance from these high interest rates. As a matter of fact, people will say: I remember Bill C-36 being introduced and passed in the House of Commons. Then I will be able to pull this Bill out of my hip pocket and say to them: Here is the Act. It does absolutely nothing to assist you. It does absolutely nothing to bring relief to people suffering from high mortgage interest rates. The Bill does nothing to encourage people to take out a home mortgage today knowing that rates will likely escalate in the months ahead. The Bill is a sham. It is an attempt to mislead the people of Canada. It is an attempt to misinform Canadians and to give them a false sense of hope and security.
In order to allow other people time to make some comments, I will bring my remarks very quickly to a close. Let me say that we had the opportunity in the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs to see some very intensive gruelling questioning by a number of Members of various officials in an effort to find out how this Bill would benefit Canadians. After a considerable period of intensive questioning by various officials such as Mr. King, others, and the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. MacLaren), we found out nothing. What we found was that this Bill would not assist the average Canadian citizen in bringing any relief from high interest rates. What came out of the committee hearing, in an effort to prepare ourselves for today, was the fact that the Government introduce a Bill to try to respond to the criticisms being levied against it that high interest rates were causing concern to home owners and to potential home owners. This Bill was an attempt to deflect some of that criticism and to say: Yes, we have passed a Bill. It is called an Act to Amend the Interest Act. And the intention to bring some relief. It has done anything but that, Mr. Speaker. It has not brought any relief. It is a sham. I believe I should now call it nine o'clock.
June 28, 1984

subtopic: RAILWAYS-ALFALFA PRODUCTS FREIGHT RATES. (fl) REQUEST THAT MINISTER CONDUCT INVESTIGATION
RAILWAYS-ALFALFA PRODUCTS FREIGHT RATES. (fl) REQUEST THAT MINISTER CONDUCT INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this adjournment debate concerns the question of railway freight rates for alfalfa products shipped by railway containers, specifically by Tirol Dehydrators of Tilley and Rolling Hills in southern Alberta. The reference is my question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) on May 29, 1984, as reported at page 4181. This is the second occasion on which I have brought the matter to the attention of the Minister of Transport.
I should like to give a brief review of the developments in this issue involving the shipment of dehydrated alfalfa cubes in containers to Japan. As a result of a favourable recommendation emerging from Bill C-155 last year, that is the Crow debate, alfalfa products were recognized as a specialty crop and became eligible for the new so-called Crow rate, effective January 1, 1984. Prior to this date all such alfalfa products paid full commercial freight rates for railway hopper cars, boxcars or containers. The Minister of Transport personally supported recognition of alfalfa as a specialty crop. Regardless of this new recognition, railways continued to charge commercial rates because the product was being moved in containers rather than in boxcars or hopper cars.
Following my first question last January, the Minister requested the CTC to instruct railways to use the authorized, lower new Crow rate for container shipments, and apparently the railways complied. However, in May the railways applied to the CTC for additional surcharges of $400 for 40-foot containers and $241 for 20-foot containers, retroactive to January 1, 1984. The CTC rejected these surcharges on May 23.
During June, this month, the railways persisted and informed Tirol that they intended to charge a lower $230 surcharge for containers effective August 1, 1984, when the new crop year begins. At this stage railways were still trying to increase their freight charges, even though they were told twice not to do so by the CTC.
Also this month the railway indicated that they will go to court, probably next October, for authority to charge demurrage fees on alfalfa and all other new specialty crops included in the Western Grain Transportation Act. We should note that original Crow crops did not have demurrage charges since they were protected by Order in Council. It would seem that the new specialty crops were never added to that Order in Council list. There is also an additional "positioning charge" now being
Adjournment Debate
imposed by the railways. If the shipping customer fails to pay the positioning charge of $253 and $127, for the two sizes of containers, a shortage of containers develops-one pays or goes short. The only positive development in this alfalfa saga is that satisfactory minimum tonnage limits have now been resolved for both west and east container movements.
In my question of May 29 to the Minister of Transport, I made the blunt statement that "The railways are obviously playing games here". The Minister concurred with my comments. Surely it is now appropriate for the CTC to rule that alfalfa products as a new specialty crop come under the authority of the Western Grain Transportation Act, not under the Railway Act. It seems so obvious that the railways are deliberately going out of their way to circumvent not only the details of the new Crow agreement but, perhaps more importantly, the spirit of this new commodity approach that had such positive and enthusiastic support during the Crow debate last year by all on the standing committee, especially by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy).
Tirol Dehydrators are presently in a serious quandary, resulting from an improper surcharge bill that totalled $336,000, and have found it prudent to drastically reduce their Japanese shipments from around 11,000 tonnes to about 500 tonnes per month, and the competition in the United States is picking up the difference. Tirol Dehydrators in southern Alberta are experienced and competent, with over eight years of trading with Japan. Their management team of Alex Chrumka and Ike Schroder deserve something much better than this railway runaround.
[ Translation]

subtopic: TRADE-TEXTILE AND CLOTHING IMPORTS-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO PROTECT JOBS
TRADE-TEXTILE AND CLOTHING IMPORTS-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO PROTECT JOBS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Regan) to explain and reconfirm his answer in the House that the Celanese plant in Coaticook is not modern enough and worse, that polyester imports do not come from countries where prices are lower than they are in Canada, and that we must develop modern and competitive plants, something Celanese failed to do in Coaticook, which has only eighty modern looms out of a total of 801. I am saying this because there is a tendency to put all the blame on the Government, and also because failing to counter often gratuitous charges would not only mean admitting the Government is wrong, but also discourage other textile workers and employers who have been, or will be, doing what must be done to maintain the textile sector, which can and must be kept as a viable and even a dynamic and stable industry. I therefore insist that we look at the facts, and if we do, we shall see that part of the responsibility lies with the industry. Personally, I believe we must preserve our textile industry, and I believe it can be done.
Mr. Speaker, it is therefore vital that the Minister establish exactly what the facts are, so that workers in Coaticook will be told the truth, and we must also provide reassurances for other textile manufacturers who are anxious to adjust to market requirements with plants that are modern and truly competitive. This is particularly important, because what is involved here is the political will of the Government of Canada and also the new decisions the Government will have to make to act in a manner consistent with the extended mandate of the Canadian Industrial Renewal Board.
The Government has already made it clear that the textile, clothing and footwear industries and the jobs they provide were very important, but also that adjustments were needed to guarantee a market and especially to provide guarantees within a normal national and international market situation, without undue and costly artificial intervention by the Government itself. The textile problem is a complex one, even textile workers realize this-but in Coaticook, they are no longer willing to stand up for an industry they kept going because of their sacrifices, because today, they realize that all their efforts have gone down the drain, now the company wants to reorganize or owing to strictly financial considerations such as maximum profits, which ignore the fact that people in a community depend on the industry for jobs. It makes matters even worse when we have workers like those in Coaticook who have reached maximum productivity, at a time when the company should have adjusted its technology to be truly competitive.
Mr. Speaker, I would, however, like to note the generosity of a number of Celanese executives, who wanted to offer workers some kind of compensation by giving them the plant building,
which is certainly a considerable advantage for the Town of Coaticook which may, in turn, use the building to attract industry and so replace the jobs that were lost. Before turning over a new page, however, I want those workers who gave the best years of their lives to the Celanese plant in Coaticook, and younger workers who were already applying their skills in the plant to be fully and accurately informed about what is happening in their industry.
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of these comments is not to point the finger of guilt at another party, it is to ensure that all parties concerned, especially the workers, have access to the same facts when accepting a decision that has become inevitable. These workers cannot be allowed to be the victims of such a decision. All responsible parties in Coaticook must be committed to providing alternative solutions, involving the co-operation and approval of the workers, in order to preserve their economic stability and to find new jobs as necessary.
To avoid giving workers the impression that they are just pawns in an industrial chess game, I think the solution to their problem lies in dialogue and understanding, and they are entitled to full information. To me, it is the only way to create the atmosphere of trust that is a prerequisite for finding a solution to the problem.
Can the Parliamentary Secretary, speaking for the Minister who knows the industry and its present and future requirements, inform the House what other reasons there were besides those given to justify closing the Celanese plant in Coaticook? In other words, to what extent is Celanese justified in putting the blame on imports alone, and should the company not admit that its reluctance to invest is now obliging it to reconsider its own priorities for achieving maximum profits, and thus to reorganize, restructure and even relocate, while turning an almost blind eye to the present and the past?

subtopic: BILINGUALISM-EDUCATION OF IMMIGRANT CHILDREN. (B) NATIVE INDIAN CHILDREN-ACCESS TO ABORIGINAL LANGUAGE EDUCATION
BILINGUALISM-EDUCATION OF IMMIGRANT CHILDREN. (B) NATIVE INDIAN CHILDREN-ACCESS TO ABORIGINAL LANGUAGE EDUCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago I addressed two questions to the Secretary of State (Mr. Joyal). I pointed out that in a number of our larger cities, Montreal, Winnipeg, Vancouver and Toronto to mention a few, there are a substantial number of students who just are not making it. They have not got the background and the command of the official languages which permit them to keep up with their classes and to get the education which they need if they are to succeed as adults in our society.
Who are these students? They are immigrant children, children who come from families who have come to Canada from countries where they speak neither English nor French, and the language which is spoken at home is a language which is not used in our schools or in our society as a whole, or, they are Native children. Native people have been moving into our cities in very large numbers.
The immigrant children are here because the federal Government encouraged immigration from the countries from which they came. Native children are in our cities because Native people have been leaving the reserves in very large numbers. Both of these groups of children are finding it very difficult to succeed in obtaining the education which they need.
Country-wide testing is done. There is a test which is called the Canadian Basic Skills Test. It was recently applied in Winnipeg. It was found that in the core area of Winnipeg- and it is true in other cities, I am sure-the schools which are largely populated by immigrant and Native children had test scores which were disastrously low. They were as low as 5 per cent or 10 per cent on a scale of 100 per cent. The average pass mark is 50 per cent.
By the time these children reach Grade 6, many of them are only reading at a Grade 3 or Grade 4 level. The result is that they fall further and further behind as more pressure is put on them in the higher grades. Many of them leave school. In fact, it is very clear that a high percentage of these students never finish high school.
We are in a period of time when society demands that young people entering the job market need to know a great deal more than ever before. They must have a firm foundation, not just in language, but in mathematics and in some of the sciences. These young people are doomed to failure. They are the immediate losers, but society as a whole will be the loser for generations to come because these young people who are not receiving adequate education simply cannot succeed.
Adjournment Debate
The Minister answered my questions by saying that the federal Government was already involved in helping to finance the education of these people by a program known as English as a second language. The program is working. In the City of Winnipeg, 1,100 immigrant children and 1,500 Native children are participating in that program.
The Minister is wrong if he thinks that all that is needed is help through the program for English as a second language. A great deal more is needed if those young people are to be brought up to the standards which society demands. There is a need for more teachers' aids and special work books which relate to immigrant and native children and their cultural backgrounds. The hours need to be longer so that these children can be helped to make up the difference in their shortcomings and their backgrounds. We need teachers who are trained to meet the multicultural challenge. The parents need to be helped to learn the language and to learn more about our history, particularly the mothers who do not go out to work, many of whom will never learn either the English or French language. What is required is a tremendous effort on the part of the local school district. But, Mr. Speaker, they do not have the financial ability to meet the requirements, and neither do the provinces.
What I am urging the Minister and the Government to do is to face up to their responsibilities. I know that the constitutional responsibility for education rests with the provinces. However, the children I talk about are there because the federal Government encouraged them to be there. I say that the federal Government should accept its moral responsibility and help to finance the educational programs which are needed to help these young people fit into our society and become full citizens, able to take their places as they should.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: BILINGUALISM-EDUCATION OF IMMIGRANT CHILDREN. (B) NATIVE INDIAN CHILDREN-ACCESS TO ABORIGINAL LANGUAGE EDUCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in replying to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), when he mentions the requirements of children whose language spoken at home is neither English or French, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts) has already made arrangements with his provincial colleagues to renegotiate the federal-provincial agreement on the citizenship and language instruction agreement, as well as the language text book agreement. The impetus for renegotiation of the agreements has come from the Treasury Board, which expressed concern over the "open-ended" nature of the agreement; from the provinces, who reviewed these agreements in 1980 with a view to renegotiating the needs of these particular children; and from the community, which following an immigrant women's conference in Toronto in 1981 gave a report which is reflected in these recommendations.
At present there is a departmental discussion paper drafted and there are consultations under way with CEIC, the Ministry of State for Social Development, the Treasury Board Secretariat and the federal-provincial relations office. Following the completion of consultations with the central agencies

June 28, 1984
Adjournment Debate
and other federal departments, a memorandum will be sent to Cabinet to be drafted for ministerial attention within the next two months. A major decision will then be taken to consider the approach and timing for negotiation of these agreements.
When we speak of the native children, the Secretary of State (Mr. Joyal) tries to address the needs of native children not addressed by the DIAND. The recommendations presented to the Secretary of State were that native children must be assured of instruction in their native language, customs and heritage, as well as in the official language of their parent's choice. This is being done by improving training opportunities for teachers of native languages; furthering development of native language curriculum; developing of written materials in
the field of native languages for use in schools and communities; and strengthening of cultural identity through improved ability to communicate in native languages. Provincial and territorial departments of education and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development must be required to support and provide adequate funding for innovative educational programs such as survival schools and other alternate schools.
